translations.text: Discourses on the beneficent providence of God.
By Anton of Tagrit, surnamed Gurgan.
Through the power of the adorable and uncreated Trinity, we write the discourses on the beneficent providence of God.
Showing and explaining how, without compelling free will, it restrains it from stumbling and from the fruits of sin. Composed by Anton, the monk of Tagrit.
Out of compassion for pure consciences, which are troubled about God's pure providence and greatly disturbed,
and which earnestly ask questions, we have therefore come forward, so that through an explanatory discourse, illuminated by the light of the fathers and of God,
[?], and thus, while passing over the lofty depths of unsearchable knowledge in ancient silence.
And let no one bring against us the charge of loving investigation, controversy, and disputes over words,
because, although zeal for beneficent providence still possesses us, we have thought fit to examine this without [?] or error, and beyond the reproach of many.
For tongues delight in heaping abuse upon everything praiseworthy. They make it their concern and labor
to drag everything down into humiliation. When someone takes care to enrich himself with the good that comes from contemplation, they call him arrogant,
a lover of honor, and a seeker of empty glory. But if, again, he wishes to preserve accuracy in the subjects of study,
and to hold reverence to be something that cannot be taught, and on this basis to establish himself as an interpreter of the sacred writings,
or of the praises of those who are great and renowned in philosophy, there they call him a disputant, a contradictor, a quarrelsome man, and an inquisitor.
Or rather, an energetic, virtuous lover of wisdom! Likewise, even if he bears the excellence of the holy disciplines and joins himself to humility
and to the purity that comes from vigils, and, in a word, clothes himself in all the watchfulness of ascetic life,
they call such a man a pretender, false to his profession, and an impostor, and no longer a philosopher.
Therefore, as for these foolish and insipid words, which stand far removed from goodness and virtue—or rather, which, under the appearance of goodness, deprive people of the good of loving hard work—
to despise and disregard them is an exercise in divine things. So much for all this; for I have no concern to contend with tongues
that are wanton. Rather, I will turn to the subject toward which the discourse was pressing, explaining what the reason is
that, while providence and care surround our affairs, violent deaths are inflicted and many murders are brazenly committed,
and many suffer departure from this life before their time, and unusual rains are brought upon us, and plagues in the air sweep around the regions,
together with tremors and earthquakes, conflagrations, and violent outbursts of fire that arise from the ether.
These things, and a multitude of others, are what this discourse intends to unfold and explain one after another.
First, then, let us say this openly: there is nothing deprived of providence or left destitute of it.
Rather, God, who is good by nature, takes account equally and universally of the [?] and the wicked, the unclean and the pure.
He does not, because of rebellion and transgression, immediately turn in anger to neglect, like someone enraged at the wicked.
Nor does he withdraw his hand from the good because of their diligence and observance of the holy commandments, as though they were sufficient by themselves to attain complete perfection.
Rather, like an intelligible sun, and as the creator of perceptible light, he grants all beings a sound existence together with abundant care.
But if a sinful mind and an evil understanding, whether among human beings or demons, sink into everything reprehensible and shameful, it is fitting to know
that providence is by no means the cause of this suffering, but rather the mind that loves deceit. But if someone should say,
“Why, when providence exists, does it allow the wicked to speak such things? For it ought to restrain the hand of the insolent,
hobble the steps of the wanton, check the onslaught of robbers, and put an end to the deceitful words of deceivers and the destructive counsels of Belial.
Indeed, it should uproot every harmful root when it sprouts, or prevent it before it comes into being”—let that person hear this answer, which is not unjust:
Providence is assigned to existing things in two ways. In one way, it watches over and cares for everything, as things that from the beginning
were established and brought into existence by the Creator’s word. In the other, when something decays and falls away from a sound and harmonious condition, it brings it back
to its own original state. We can see something comparable to this among certain craftsmen who are our fellow human beings,
particularly among physicians who treat illness. For the physician, opposing the weakness of nature, exercises care and concern in two ways.
First, he acts so that the body itself will not be afflicted with the weakness caused by illness. Accordingly, he proceeds to provide suitable foods,
so that it will not fall into danger of illness through the poor quality of its food. We know these things,
we who attend the lavish tables of rulers. Then, if some bodily humor has increased and become excessive in the body,
and the body has consequently become prone to illness, he supports and strengthens it through purgative medicines made from roots. So too does the Lord, who abounds in help.
For, having brought everything into existence from being [?], he cares for it in a most saving and divine manner, as things that come from the beginning.
Thus, into angelic beings and beings endowed with souls he pours immortality and supremely excellent knowledge.
To material and bodily beings he gives succession from one another and change that preserves and sustains their nature; and to plants he gives growth and fruit.
And to the [?] he gives stability, good constancy, cohesion with one another, freedom from diminution, and continued existence [?] of the others.
Therefore, freedom too—which is authority over oneself, that is, our ability to carry out as masters whatever we wish among the things within our power,
whether evil or good—you preserve [?] the original word. And he watches over this and takes care that it is not altered or destroyed.
Its destruction and alteration would consist in this: if someone wished to think, speak, desire, or carry something out,
and could think and do what is virtuous, but could not do the contrary things at all, or, though able, were disciplined so as not to think of experiencing them.
For if someone rebels and becomes obstinate, and is forcibly and compulsorily restrained from the impulse and desire to marry, how can this person, who possesses freedom, be accused?
For freedom is not something that comes under the constraints of compulsion and oppression. That is a kind of servile submission.
Rather, it is that which stands outside the yoke of necessity and coercion and has the authority to go [?] wherever it wishes and wherever it pleases,
whether in the desirable conduct of virtue or in the detestable conduct of wickedness. For because they have a succession through their constant transformation into one another,
they no longer diminish. They say that earth, when it becomes thinner, changes into water, and that water, when heated and increased, is broken down into air,
and air, in turn, into fire. Conversely, fire, when it becomes denser, changes into air, and air into water, and water, when it becomes compact and dense, into earth.
Consequently, neither decrease nor increase affects them. This is what those called natural philosophers say.
And the blessed Gregory of Nyssa, in the discourse he wrote on the spiritual exposition of his brother Basil’s Six Days,
where, that is, he puts both us, human beings who are bound, and the unbound nature of incorporeal beings on an equal footing:
whether one speaks of the good angels or of the darkness of demons and destroyers, this is the benefit that providence gives us:
that, by virtue of self-rule and freedom, we live and subsist, think and speak, are stirred to action and carry it through.
But if we were to suffer a fall from this too, it is clear that we would also be removed from the distinctive character of our nature.
The distinctive property and distinguishing mark of incorporeal nature is rationality, and its fruit is thought.
What characterizes thought is not, of course, to consider this but not that, or to have knowledge of the one—
that is, the good—but not of the other, that is, evil. Rather, it considers things that exist and things that do not exist,
things established and things expected, things true and things false, things harmful and things beneficial. It considers and reflects on them, and consequently either holds firm or gives way.
This, then, is the good of incorporeal nature. And toward this, God’s providence, full of benefits,
should fittingly show its care: toward that which, if we lose it, we ourselves are lost.
We would have to sink into a nature [?], a nature without reason, [?], and become like high-humped camels and like the elephant, a tower of flesh.
These are generally guided by a single impulse. This is implanted in them through a natural movement: namely, to shrink back from things that harm
their constitution, whether in feeding or in traveling or in any other need, and in turn to approach
things that help and benefit them. This happens not through reflection and thought, but through being driven and impelled by nature.
And when it is hungry, it does not refrain from feeding if food is available. And when, in particular, it recalls lustful desire, it rushes forward.
It also turns aside from pits and holes and from every deadly plant, not through discernment and judgment,
but through the benefit arising from desire, whether from smells or sights, which is bound up with it and accompanies it.
So that we should not become like these and fall short of the goodness of our nature, providential justice makes provision.
For this reason, it does not restrain the soul’s thoughts, the murderous and deceitful plans of evildoers, or the course taken by murderers and those who act immorally with women.
At certain times, and for certain people, however, it does so—and then not the thoughts, but rather the deeds, and where this is most beneficial.
For we know of someone who, on one occasion, when he had emboldened himself to commit foul murder or had approached a defiled bed, was hindered by certain circumstances.
He had indeed thought and reflected. Once he had stirred up the impulse of his will, he did not prolong his deliberation. He decided [?] and pursued what was full of shame.
He was deprived only of the completion of the act. Although free will had been active in these things, its impetus [?] was blunted when the matter came to its outcome.
In this way free will was easily diverted toward what was beneficial, as has been said: either for the sake of the person acting,
or for the sake of the person suffering, or for the sake of both together, as he who is supremely good himself knows.
Perhaps someone, pursuing the argument set out above, will say that free will can indeed remain self-determining
and yet think and feel only these things, loving and accomplishing what is fitting and brings us salvation, either through its own understanding or through God’s protection.
To this objector we say: How, then, do you mean that freedom of will can adhere only to what is right?
Is it as though some necessity were yoked to it, not allowing it to turn toward shameful things?
Or is it that, being acquainted with evil and knowing good, it keeps its distance from the former as harmful, but pursues the latter with all its
strength as beneficial? If you take the first meaning, our freedom and capacity for choice disappear—
that equal inclination toward evil or good which we demonstrated above. But if you mean the second, we say
that it is possible, while retaining authority over ourselves, to pursue all the excellent practices of holiness and to keep entirely away from faults and errors.
The souls of holy people who live in purity, and the ranks and companies of the good powers, convince us of this.
So much, then, for the claim that free will can be directed toward good alone through its own understanding. But if this comes from God, it must be one of two things:
either he guides and leads it through pure commandments and prudent counsels, or he hinders and prevents it from rushing toward or pursuing detestable things.
This hindering, in turn, has two forms: either he prevents evil’s first birth by keeping our mind from even contemplating it,
or, through certain obstructing circumstances, he renders its mind inactive in this matter. But if someone asks that, both by awakening the conscience [?] and by discipline,
the Good One should destroy the birth of evil within us, his providence has never ceased to show that it dwells [?] among us.
Rather, in every manner and by every means, he has diligently sought to destroy the root of sin within us: at one time through seers and prophets,
and at another through angels sent out, through counsels, through threats [?], through the establishment of laws, and through judgment.
But if someone says that he ought not to have allowed the root of evil to sprout within us in the first place, this again leads to the destruction of the will’s self-determination.
Since, indeed, it is not possible for us to be deprived of the ability to think evil, seeing that we were created as thinking beings.
And this is not evil. For it is not thinking that is forbidden, but thinking after passing judgment and knowing that it is evil,
and deliberately either dwelling on it or carrying it out. And if we were stirred only by good thoughts, and not otherwise,
we would have [?] that goodness is preserved in us as a fruit of nature, just as fire [?] makes many upward leaps,
and water has a downward-rolling rush. And if someone will not say this, it must be like something rejected [?].
But let us seek what restrains the impulse. Again, we speak of one of two things: either tyrannically and forcibly, or through hindrances
and obstacles. And through obstacles, again, in two ways: either through bitter rods of correction,
or through intervening shoals and crags—that is, to speak plainly, the failure of undertakings.
And if someone proposes the tyrannical way, he is mistaken. For our God is good and does not wish to force freedom. If he does force it, he destroys it.
Only occasionally and rarely, perhaps, does he resort to this, as when he restrains the hosts of demons from harming our nature or people whose conduct is honorable.

For he rebukes and sternly reprimands their power, as we know from the Scriptures, so that they will not harm the saints. Zechariah knows this, as does the book of that illustrious man, and the Gospel concerning Legion.
Likewise, he sometimes brings compulsion upon those human beings who act unjustly, granting victory to what benefits the greater number,
and to some extent restraining and coercing freedom. Yet he does not do so altogether, so that freedom should cease to exist, nor even for the most part. Let the book of Kings convince you.
For the hand that he stretched out against him withered. In the same way, Moses says that he brings destruction and obliteration upon certain people utterly given over to injustice.

There is also the destruction of the lustful Sodomites, the merciless inundation of the Egyptians, the drowning of the [?] in the days of Noah, and the gaping mouth of the beast of the earth because of the wicked Dathan and Abiram.
There is [?] and the death of young people and children, together with hidden miscarriages, which we continually see those mighty mercies of the Father bringing about.
These things happen through compulsion, as the argument has shown. Nevertheless, the adversary too is left with freedom of will,
since he is sometimes restrained from causing overwhelming destruction, but human beings are not. For he incites many to anger, and advises and persuades them.
He brings them down through unbelief and idolatrous error, leads them astray through desire, deceives them through falsehood, and alienates them through many vices
and murders [?]. Likewise, weak human beings, being incited through their freedom, have passed into every kind of injustice and shamefulness.
The power of compulsion did not come upon them, nor did coercion keep their freedom in check. They chose and, according to their ability, fulfilled their desire for destruction.
This, however, is what one says when explaining restraint through compulsion. As for restraint through scourges and corrective discipline, again
we speak in contrast to the demonstration concerning compulsion. For there we said that the Good One rarely resorts to using compulsion.
For the most part, however, he relaxes his hold and leaves the free mind to itself. Here, by contrast, he sends obstacles through discipline abundantly and frequently.
Only rarely does he delay or neglect these things. Sometimes, when someone is striving to prevail, he subjects him to illnesses that are difficult to cure.
And often these people do not even have a natural impulse, as we know that many grow weak and fall ill,
whether from fullness or cold, from emptiness or exhaustion. Rather, the one who disciplines them sometimes acts beforehand, when a person plans to defile himself,
and sometimes when the readiness of his mind brings this about, or at the very beginning of an occasion for evil.
But through his providence, which sustains everything, he permits another person to be tormented by punishing demons,
either judging and rebuking future wickedness, as in the case of children, or making an example of excessive ungodliness and wickedness
in those who did not take his patience as a reason to return and did not repent of their wickedness. He also disciplines others by taking away their wealth,
if it becomes material for wickedness and fuel for anger and lust in a person, removing his instrument, as a judge does to a robber’s hands.
Such are those who are robbed, or whose ships’ cargoes sink, or whose cattle and flocks perish.
He also allows the mind to fall into a lowly condition when he sees the suffering caused by pride,
as in the case of [?], or so that a person may not be cast into the defilement of heresies and appear to someone else as a sign of destruction.
Again, he permits someone highly skilled in his craft to be weakened by another affliction, so that a claim to divinity and conceit may not destroy him.
In short, our God, who cares for everything, subjects many people to varied forms of discipline.
And someone might say in response to this: Why, when discipline is destined to be so beneficial, does it not fall upon all the wicked alike and draw them out of the depths of their misery?
And again, why [?] does it not come to the very same person many times, so that he may be shown to be free of all wickedness?
Let us bring this remedy and bandage to this question: he knows the things that are to come and all things—
he who cares for everything. Or is there something else? I do not know that there is anything else to say.
Therefore, when he foresees that someone will gain abundant benefits from the rod of discipline and, through sound judgment, desist from wickedness, he benefits that person through discipline.
But someone who, either through an excessive desire to do evil or through a violent inclination, becomes worse through forms of discipline—this person he leaves without correction.
It is known that discipline is harmful to some people. For we know this from an account: two men went astray and committed adultery.
One was disciplined by a fever for six months, received correction from the blow, and attained profound virtue.
But the other, though disciplined by a quartan fever and severe pains from the blows of judgment,
did not at all quiet or lower his adulterous thoughts, but fulfilled his wicked desire whenever he found relief from this illness.
And because, like that fool, he engaged in these deeds and did not accept correction from rebukes, he prepared many blows for justice to inflict.

For this person, then, which do you judge would have been helpful: to be left wandering in the distraction of lust, or to be disciplined, when the Good One knew beforehand that he would never desist from wickedness?
For in the former case he would have been liable to one stroke and one sentence; but in the latter he becomes liable to two punishments.
There, it was a matter of the man being defiled when he committed fornication; here, however, it is both his being defiled and his becoming resentful at the discipline.
But someone says, “Why, then, was such a man disciplined through Acticus?” Because of the goodness of providence, which did not leave him without discipline.
“And how should he be liable to only one punishment? For here, according to your argument, providence itself has harmed him.”
To these objections the true account replies that it is not to all such people that the Lord sends death as a disciplining rod—
the Lord. For we also see many practitioners of [?], as well as murderers and violent men,
who [?] have grown old without distress and have passed their lives free from every danger.
But if he disciplines some of them, as with the man included in the illustration, he does not act in this way without reason or justice. For because
many accuse and blame providence, looking at the wickedness and depravity being practiced and asking why it did not bring judgment upon the offender and restrain him,
so that he might abandon this wickedness; or, again, because the offender himself, after fulfilling his desire and coming to his senses, may afterward reflect,
“Why did he not bring some discipline upon me and stop me? If he had wished, deliverance would have followed”—because of thoughts like these,
providence would stand accused in another way, and they would be harmed by such thinking and speech.
For this reason he afflicts and disciplines once or twice, and then lowers the hand he had raised,
so that through this one person he may teach that it would have been just for all his companions in wickedness to suffer. But because they do not stop doing evil at all,
even if discipline hangs over them, he leaves them, so that through the destruction of the one being punished many may become heirs. And precisely for this reason,
he strengthens the hand of conscience: “I would not have stumbled.” But when he was neglected by providence, he fell into grumbling; and not many, again, when they [?],
ask why the wicked prosper, when they see that those whom they envy have been harmed by discipline rather than benefited.
For if two people are accused of [?]—counterfeiters or burglars—and one of them falls into the judge’s hands,
while the other finds an escape, and the first is flogged and suffers loss, and his foot is put in the stocks for long periods and his hand is bound in chains,
and his neck in an iron collar, but afterward he is released and persists in his [?], someone is wrong to make the false claim about the man who did not suffer,
“If he had been disciplined, he would have become good.” For one can challenge this by asking, “What about the man who was disciplined? Did he become good?”
No, indeed. Neither, then, would this man have experienced a change from wickedness through disciplinary measures unless it had come from his own free choice.
For he may become resentful and grow still more wicked when subjected to discipline, like a childish-minded boy who, because of a whipping, contemplated strangling himself.
Thus, then, the law of providence has been cleared of defilement. But it is also possible to approach the interpretation set out earlier in another way:
the Good One, like a great physician, first casts out the causes of wickedness. One person receives complete healing, while in another no healing is apparent.

Yet his conscience is taught that the physician has not neglected any of his proper duties. And while he blames his illness for its severity, he meets the physician with gratitude and does not put him to shame.
But another, though he knows and has examined him beforehand, not only gains no recovery from the disease that grips him, but becomes increasingly angry and blames the physician.
Because he is sick in mind as well as body, he therefore blames his treatment, full of benefits. Such are all those who, when that just one disciplines them gently,
turn the method of discipline into a trade in destruction, grumbling and complaining and carrying out every kind of evil,
and, like pigs charging against goads, rush into destructive wickedness. Thus, then, the first objection raised in reply has been demolished.
It remains to show why he lifts the rod of discipline from the unfortunate man, although he knows the outcome and to what end wickedness will lead him.
For we see many who behave modestly as long as they are kept in subjection, and remain humble as long as they are sick,
but become licentious when they are freed, and puffed up when they regain their strength. And we see a leper deeply covered in white patches,
who, when health was brought to him through the help of the physician’s hand, grew large and fat and became hardened through the wickedness of desire. These things are so. But what then?
Does this perhaps leave the teaching about providence without any basis? Yet through all these things it stands ready not to become in any respect a cause of stumbling to the community.
Therefore he restrains wickedness through discipline for as long as the Lord himself knows to be good. But when he knows that, through its continuation,
the person being corrected is coming to an even greater evil, he brings it to an end and folds it away. For providential care undertakes this struggle by every means:
either that the person who is [?] to error should not sin at all, or that he should withdraw from greater errors; and third, that whatever he suffers should purify him.
To learn that someone sometimes comes to another kind of wickedness if the disciplining hand persists, consider those who run to sorcerers and magicians,
so that they may either send a demon away from someone or heal the pain in his limbs, when they have been deprived of the help of physicians.
But for others—for those for whom suffering such pains brings salvation—he brings the punishments to other outcomes:
for the pure, a crown of endurance and victory over suffering; for those easily led astray, a liberating departure; and for others, purification from the stains and errors they have committed.
But for those slipping and stumbling toward the pit of destruction, he brings their departure near and calls them out of their pain, even if the afflictions holding them are less than this.

But the lover of disputes raises a further question about these things: why, then, does he not first pass judgment on the demon or the disease [?], so that others too may receive this benefit in abundance?
For we do not rejoice whenever it is removed from someone. And so you have destroyed many, O sects of those who serve demons!
But the [?] mind rebukes these things, bringing forward the great power of free will as something at which to marvel.
For when the one who holds the reins of our nature cares for us to save us and directs the rod against us in a way intended to bring us back,
the mind, becoming agitated and refusing to bear the weight of the scourge with endurance, clings to the utmost wickedness.

For it did not turn back to the one who disciplines or humble itself before him, because he is the one who heals every pain, and he is the one who breaks and binds you up, as the holy words make clear;
nor did it recognize the purifying nature of the treatment. Instead, taking thought for its own destruction, it came to what casts it into far greater dangers.
It sought relief at the hands of those who serve demons.
And even through smoke it would have been possible for that arrogant one, when violently stirred up, to crush the person who followed this path, especially since his feet were so tender.
But he permits these things so that free choice may be tested and the weakness of faith exposed.
So when someone severely afflicted by punishment makes his way to that evil healer and priest of the demon, if indeed
his bodily disfigurement comes from a scourge sent from above, is that destructive power of the demon able to do anything at all to free him and cleanse him of his illness?
For it is impossible for him to prove capable of removing all those things imposed by the Lord as punishment.
Instead, he crushes him and doubles his pain, either because the Lord permits it or because he himself loves the corruption and destruction of our nature.

[?] Perhaps, when someone goes to seek refuge with demons, the Lord allows him to find [?] from his pain, so that, without understanding, he may become entangled in those [?] paths and become deeply committed to the worship of demons
and grow stronger in it. For a demon never leaves his dwelling in a person if he has received a command to remain there as punishment; nor does the illness depart,
if it is beneficial in this way for it not to depart, even if someone were to assemble the whole troop of demons and sorcerers as though for some battle. Experience has shown us this.
For we have seen many people being tormented, to whom certain sorcerers and diviners hurried.
Although they displayed certain apparitions, or made something like a woman speaking in a thin voice from her belly be heard,
or the demon himself formed some utterance on the tongue of the sick person, we have never seen them obtain deliverance from this scourge.
Instead, sometimes he became even more fiercely emboldened against them, or continued as before, for as long as their abandonment by God gave him room to act against them.

Understand from this that free choice and unbelief are the cause of this destruction, rather than the torment inflicted by demons. Here, for example, is someone who has been robbed and has lost everything he owned.
Another has a wife who suffers from barrenness. And while the Lord, that gracious helmsman, looks toward what is beneficial
and has made poverty beneficial for the one and childlessness for the other, they, driven by an evil impulse and with minds steeped in evil,
ask destructive demons to restore what they have lost, and ask those who are harmful in every way and are our enemies to grant them children.
But when has a demon who does evil ever brought beings into existence or created anything?
For he has an unceasing concern to destroy, but none at all to establish and sustain,
even if perhaps he possessed the power to do so. But I will return to the point pressing upon the discussion: there are many
who, sick with the feeble impulses of unbelief and driven by their sovereign free choice, have taken methods of healing
and corrective, disciplinary scourges and made them material for evil. They have turned a source of help into its opposite, a source of harm.
It is as though someone were to take the instruments of medical practice, or the weapons given him for defense against hostile attack,
misuse them and destroy himself, cutting off his fingers or his [?] with a scalpel, and applying cauterizing irons
[?] not for the weakness of his stomach, but to his eyes while they are healthy.
And he would thrust himself onto the sword and bring himself under the sharp point of the spear and onto the lance; and whoever made use of [?].
Just as, if a fracture or a very serious ulcer afflicts someone, and he approaches a physician who treats such ailments to have it bandaged,
he might readily, because of the burning caused by the poultices, bring the destruction of the knife upon his tender neck.
So, then, the good law of providence, through such forms of discipline, restrains and hinders many people from carrying their evil deeds through to completion.
For even through the failure of undertakings—what is customarily called coincidence and chance—
he holds many people back and stops them from doing wrong. We do not maintain this without reason, for we see thieves and murderers,
and corrupt people, each seized by an impulse to do evil and striving by every means to fulfill his heart’s desire.
You have observed [?] how one, after laboring all night to break in, is overtaken either by the gleam and radiance of daylight or by the household becoming aware of him.
And by taking flight, he is prevented from bringing his wickedness to completion. And a murderer, either pursuing someone or lying in ambush,
raises his sword and leaps forward with the ring [?]; then, lifting his eyes a little, he catches sight of a horseman opposite him or a troop traveling along the road.
Seized by fear, he runs away at once, without completing his wicked deed. In the same way, there is also that companion of shameful conduct.
He enters the bedroom, stirred up by evil love, and is entirely delighted that his desire is about to be fulfilled.
But what happens afterward? Someone either peers in or calls out, and in this way his entire scheme is put to shame.
In a similar way, that liar too is prevented from giving false testimony, as is the man who uses force to oppress others and takes away other people’s fields,
and others like them. But at this point someone fond of inquiry might reply, “Where is freedom?
For if, when a person is ready,” he says, “[?] in every way, and has shown every kind of delight in attaining the evil,
he afterward experiences prevention from it, against his wishes and entirely against his will, it is clear that he has been forcibly restrained.
How, then, is he free? According to your argument, then, there is no freedom in such cases.”
What, then, do we say in reply to this? The Good One holds a person back once or twice and draws him away from evil, and that is enough.
But if afterward he sees that the mind that loves wrongdoing is boldly rushing toward the deed and hurrying toward its own destruction, he lets it go and withdraws.
That is, so that his goodness may be recognized and freedom may be made manifest. For this reason we said above
that he generally restrains, and that, when appropriate, he guides by force, either for the sake of the person acting or for the sake of the person suffering. For example:
A certain woman, beautiful in appearance, was afraid of the lustful eyes of a worldly man. This chaste woman was loved, and her way of life remained continually pure.
He cast his eye upon her and [?] his wealth to the deed. He was eagerly pressing toward a love affair.

What, then, was lacking among the things that bring the attempt [?] to completion? What human devices and preparations were available? She would commit adultery, although the virgin is not moved. What, then?
It is not necessary that this act be prevented, either through correction or through an obstacle—even for the sake of the person who suffers. Yes, I know that someone says, “It certainly is.”
But even if the young man is chaste, and there is [?], the wise Lord takes no care at all to help him avoid falling, because he sees the swinishness of his mind.
Let Joseph come forward, and a certain virgin with a beautiful face, whom Diocletian loved first, and afterward Tiridates,
the kings of the Greeks and the Armenians. They overcame frenzied desire: he overcame that of corrupt women, and she overcame the forces of destruction.

Let these examples suffice concerning the person who suffers. There is also something to relate concerning the person who acts. There was a certain man, a spiritual athlete in his way of life, who was not held captive by the flesh.
While he shunned everything and stood far away from the waves of desire and the surges of anger, a certain woman of exceptional beauty became enamored of him.
For rebellious Satan was persuading her to take courage for this shameless act. She ventured to lead the courageous man astray.
She brought him into a room—he had the appearance of a merchant—and approached to indulge her passion. At that moment she was seized by punishment, as a cruel demon threw her into convulsions.
Astonished at the miracle, he gave thanks to the Savior. In this way the organizer of the contests rescued this excellent athlete from a fall. For the Righteous One spared
his great labor, so that he would not be ruined by a single mishap. But if someone says, “Look, we also see a man courageous in his discipline
who, when close to falling, was defiled and received no help,” we have already supplied the answer to this above.
For perhaps he was about to fall into pride, the most detestable of all passions; so, according to the judgments of providence, he was allowed to be humbled through a lowly passion.
There are also times when both are good, both the person acting and the person suffering, and he places an obstacle in the way of both.
And if both are evil, like two men thirsting for blood, how often he restrains them from doing wrong!
This is so that they cannot blaspheme by saying that his care for them has entirely ceased. But if this evil heart grows weary of [?], the Lord says to free will, “Rejoice!”
And as they attack one another skillfully, and their bodies are slashed by sword blows, there and then they bring destruction upon each other.
Likewise, a certain loose woman came to meet a young man whose flesh was lustful. At first the Lord restrained them once or twice,
but they were not moved to recover their senses from their impetuosity. He allowed both of them to leap upon each other like horses and suffer a miserable [?]. So much for all this.
The demonstration is sufficient, I think. But since the earlier argument had been stated as follows: when the Lord exercises providence,

whether through understanding or through preserving things that come into being, or, if they grow weak at all, renewing them with strength—and on this basis we say that he established free will in us and gave it to us as our possession,
and takes care that it should not perish, and therefore allows evil as well as good to be accomplished—we consequently asked concerning these things:
If sovereign free will is the cause of evil or good, and God is the cause of free will,
then is God the cause of both evil and good? Let us heal the person who is sick with this thought in the following way, and treat the diseased notion within him.
God is certainly not the cause of evil at all. For he is good, and the source of good things alone.
But if you insist that he is in any sense the cause of evil because he established free will in us, then, questioner, answer me this.
How is he the cause of the things that free will accomplishes, as though he were the one who moves
it to act unjustly or do evil, or to do good and act justly? How can it be said that it cannot act without God,
like a carpenter’s or a smith’s tool—a saw, a scraper, or tongs—which, without the craftsman’s own hand, does not move to saw, scrape, or grip?
But if free will stands in relation to God as a tool, it no longer remains free will at all.
For something that receives its movement and activity from another and through another is not free will.
Rather, this is the distinctive property of freedom and self-determination: to do and accomplish whatever it desires and chooses, whether praiseworthy or blameworthy.
Furthermore, if the deeds of free will are to be charged to God because he brought it into being at all,
what prevents all the deeds carried out by the devil from also being charged to God as his own?
The argument would then run like this: if the devil comes from God, but rebellion and injustice belong to the devil,
then God is also the cause of the devil’s being rebellious and wicked. This is more deplorable than anything else,
even merely to contemplate. In this way, then, we could also speak about many things that happen among us.
For example, a man fathers a beloved son, but this son becomes either dissolute or insolent and murderous. What then?
Suppose someone were to turn around and say, “Since the son is the father’s offspring, and this young man has committed adultery, his father is therefore the cause of his adultery and debauchery.”
Or, because he committed murder, his father is the cause of the bloodshed: for the son would never have come to shed blood if his father had not brought him to birth and existence.
In this way we could not charge anyone with deeds of his own, so long as someone else was the cause of his existence.
But surely, if the father is the cause of his son’s existence, he is not necessarily also the cause of these other evils. Likewise, even if God is the cause of the creation of free will,
is he thereby already the cause of its evil deeds or its good deeds? But if this idea takes hold of the mind, it becomes a web of utter impiety for human beings,
when they maintain that the Good One is the cause and source of every evil. But so that this opinion,
which is exceedingly unjust [?], may be demolished in God-loving minds, let us set out this one distinction.
The deeds of free will belong either to free will alone, to God alone, or to both jointly.
But if someone decides that they belong to God alone, free will is absolved both of the evil it has done and of the good it has performed,
and it deserves neither honor nor disgrace. But if they belong to free will alone, God is clear of being charged
as the overseer of its evil deeds [?], even though he also helps it when it performs its praiseworthy actions.
But if they come from both jointly and in combination, God appears to us weak and limited.
Or, as someone else before us concluded, God has a companion and partner in whatever he does and accomplishes—something disgraceful and thoroughly deserving of ridicule.
Along with these claims, then, comes this: either both—I mean God and free will—are guilty, or both are innocent.
But these claims must be rejected. For even if free will comes from God, its contrary activities do not therefore come from God.
Rather, it is like the power of sight in the eyes: although it receives its existence from the sun, the sun grants only the ability to see.
But seeing in this way or that is not the responsibility of the giver; it belongs to the eye itself, whether it looks at black things or white things,

or gazes at ugly things or beautiful things. No one thinking rightly says that because the eye behaved shamelessly, the sun made it shameless, or that because it wandered off into the distance, the sun made it wander.
For the sun is the cause only of its seeing. Whether it looks far away or nearby, shamelessly or modestly, belongs to the eye itself.
So too is the rule of divine providence. That free will has the capacity to act belongs to its cause.
But that it acts in this way or that, deliberately and knowingly—that is, toward licentiousness or modesty, falsehood or truth, pride or humility—
not at all. Indeed, when someone does good, God shows approval and gives help; but when someone practices evil, he shows aversion and hatred.
Thus, then, God is the cause of free will and its power, but free will itself, and not God, is the cause of the kinds of actions it performs.
Consequently, even if God is the cause of free will, God is not therefore also the cause of its activity. And the attempt at the objection just stated has been exposed as feeble and refuted.
“If God [?],” says the objector, “let us grant that its power of self-determination comes from itself and not from God.
But why, then, when [?] encompasses everything, does he bring into existence and sustain the wicked, who go astray through free will?
For he ought to have brought only the good into existence, whether angels or human beings—those whose free will has become good and is good for them.
Or is that Good One not all-knowing, knowing precisely beforehand their wickedness and the punishment they will inherit?
For it would have been better for them not to exist than to live in this way, to be tormented for long ages.” To these things we reply:
It is precisely through goodness beyond reckoning that the Lord himself brings them into existence and sustains them, even though he knows and foresees the wickedness of the evil.
For perfect goodness consists in this: creating not only those who are going to become good, but also those who are prepared to act unjustly.
Or, if it were possible, should they not come into existence at all and not be enriched with free will?

Because free will has acted wickedly, and because of what is lesser and different, should what is greater and more abundant in free will be abolished, and should the Good One thereby be shown to be not good?
For is the substance and existence of each being a good thing, yes or no? Clearly, you will say that it is good, if you think rightly.
Likewise, we have also acknowledged that free will is a good thing, when we set out the account of it in general.
What, then, would it have been fitting for the Good One to do: to bring substance [?] and free will into existence,
even if free will was going to go astray in some respect, or to withhold these things because of the lapses and errors that arise from free will itself?
This is like someone saying, when his eyes are clouded, or there is [?] in his hearing, or his body is trembling:
that [?] it would have been right for my [?] to be removed and for hearing also to be completely destroyed.
And the body itself would pass into death and destruction. Yet it is far better for it to see and hear, and indeed to live and pass away, than
to be deprived altogether. For someone whose understanding is not unjust, it is then like saying that, because freedom sometimes goes astray
and, through its transgression and wickedness, becomes a cause of punishment for human beings or for rebellious demons, they ought not to have been brought into existence.
It is like someone foolishly saying about water: because in a river or a stream, or generally in a body of flowing water,
someone drowned while swimming, and the waters became a cause of a person's destruction, water ought not to have come into existence.
Or because the sun's rays darken the eyes of certain animals and scorch tender blossoms,
the sun itself ought not to continue to exist. Yet the nature of water is good and sustains life,
and the sun is gentle on the eyesight of many and helpful in every such respect. It is also like someone saying about medicine [?]
that it is destructive, or rather opposed to nature, because it destroyed someone who used it badly, and that medicine ought not to have entered our world.
Consequently, those who put forward this comparison desire their God to be evil,
so that he should not do what he knows to be good because of the evil that accompanies it, even though he is admittedly not the cause of that evil.
For I say this with an understanding that is not unjust: it is fitting for God to bring a being into existence with freedom, even if that freedom is destined to act altogether unjustly,
since he himself is not the cause of its acting unjustly. But you who love contentiousness, what further absurdity is there here [?]?

That it would have been right for them not to have been brought into existence because they were destined to live this way, and that what abounds in goodness should be abolished because of what follows in the way of evils?
In other words, you are saying this: because I am going to prove barren, God should not be good and should not show in me the fruit of his love for humanity.
And along with the injustice and wickedness of the rest, you are heaping blasphemy and actual reproach upon your own miserable head.
But perhaps someone who disputes the argument of truth will say: if, then, from [?] original goodness, the Good One brings into being even those who are destined
to act wickedly, what prevents him, while exercising the same abundance of goodness, from showing them to be exempt [?] from punishment and making them members of the household of blessedness?

To this we say that he brought the wicked into existence and established them not only from the abundant outpouring of his goodness, but also so that goodness itself should not be diminished and rendered barren.
In one respect, this comes from the outpouring of excellence; in another, from the fullness and perfection of excellence itself.
The former concerns his refraining from bringing them into existence when he knows infallibly that they will sin; the latter concerns the fact that, if he does not bring them into existence
and does not show them to be in possession of those things that are truly good—existence [?] and freedom—his goodness is judged deficient and incomplete.

That is, if it was necessary for him to create so that his goodness might be known to its recipient, it was also necessary for him to do at once everything that he knows to be good for that recipient.
But if, after he made them and endowed them with being and the power both to exist and to exist well, those weak human beings and evil angels subsequently
They fall short of the Lord’s will, abandon a pure life, and concern themselves with things that harm life.
Since they have been negligent here and have willingly neglected virtue, anyone who seeks to make them its heirs even against their will does wrong and deprives them of freedom.
For freedom is the power within us to desire and choose either evil things or good things.
And if it chooses and desires evil things, it is not right for anyone forcibly to [?] it away from these things and lead it by compulsion, when it desires impure conduct
and idolatrous error. For through these things sin holds sway over earthly people. And we say that their recompense is this:
namely, blindness to the knowledge of God, which they loved even here. For they chose not to know God.
And through their deeds and their worship, they also make themselves worthy to inherit the confusion that they loved and cherished
in the world beyond. And if someone should turn freedom away from the shameful things it has desired, whether here or in the world beyond,
by force, he wrongs freedom and drives it away from what it is.
Therefore, if freedom, because of its desire for evil, knowingly scorns the torments appointed for it,
and indeed prefers those torments for the sake of the little pleasure available here, it is right that it should not be wronged.
For even here we see these very things happening, as among those dissolute young men. For when one of them

is aroused and, driven by a wretched desire, commits adultery and acts licentiously, he actually prefers to receive the punishment of death so that he may satisfy the wretched desire that has grown strong within him.
We have seen this happen to many people. We have also learned of it from widely circulated histories, as in the accounts of Paris and Helen,
and of the beloved sons of Priam and the mighty warrior Achilles: the destruction of death befell them because of shameful desire.
And to recall an example from my own people, consider Samson, that great source of strength for the Israelites, who, because of the folly of desire,
preferred to fall away from the Spirit, from dominion, from judicial authority, from honor, and from mighty strength, merely to increase his pleasure. We have also mentioned this:
something that happened in our own time, concerning a young man who strove to enter the king’s bedchamber and enjoy himself with his concubines.
When he was caught, he was cut apart limb by limb. We have also heard and seen similar things concerning hot-tempered men,
who, because of an insolent man [?], rose up to the sky and went down to the depths of Sheol, because they could not endure the impulse of anger.
They grew bold and cursed the king. And why should I recount many examples, when it is well known that many people
desire and prefer destruction and obliteration—both the mortal kind here and the complete kind in the world beyond—provided only that their passion is satisfied?
This, then, is freedom’s choice. If it is compelled and driven away from what it desires, it is wronged.
Therefore, so that it may not suffer this, it is indeed right that the wicked should inherit fire. Otherwise, if
recompense is not measured and apportioned to the wicked according to their deeds, justice is deficient in a very great respect.
First, as we consider this question, we see how a person commits every kind of injustice: he commits sexual immorality, defiles himself, murders, and becomes polluted.
He blasphemes and acts wickedly. Which, then, is just in these circumstances: that he should receive severe punishment for such deeds, or that he should share in the delight and rest of the saints?
But if, so that goodness may be debased, the polluted are to inherit the delight of the holy, what prevents the entire company of kings and the congregation of the righteous
from raising a rebellious neck against that Good One, so that, when everything is yoked beneath the burdens of sin,
the Good One may be known as still more gracious? In this way goodness itself would become material for wickedness—a thing that is utterly shameful and ridiculous.
Next, if we consider the other matter—I mean when we see the blood of the righteous being poured out without restraint,
and the acts of oppression committed under the sun, and the devastation and plundering, together with the whole range of other injuries—
if justice does not judge these things in the world beyond, and vigilance does not do what is fitting, then those who suffered are being wronged and oppressed.
For here the law of providence neither rebuked the wicked nor exacted punishment from them.
Moreover, the account of providence is deficient if the wicked do not drain the cup of their guilt in the world beyond. One of these conclusions follows readily.
For if the Merciful One pours out forgiveness there upon those who have acted wickedly,
why does he take it upon himself to rebuke wickedness here? Again, why did he send his Only Son as Savior, to bring us out from under the yoke of Belial, the destroyer of souls?
For what reasons did he establish laws against transgressors, bending and bringing down their [?] toward wickedness?
Or again, for what reason did he bring a violent blow and severe scourges upon unjust people here, while leaving other wrongdoers entirely alone,
if he employs mercy there, and not judgment and scourges? For an inquiry or objection of this kind requires that he either call everyone to account here
or call no one at all to account, reserving correction for the world beyond. Or what is the reason that one person, though the whole measure of his perversity was full, escaped without a scourging,
while another was struck with countless scourges here, if both are treated equally there?
For the person who suffered here is wronged by this providence, when his counterpart is deemed worthy of relief from [?] there.
Rather, it is his own free will that desires that this person should be corrected here.
For many plead and long to suffer here for their wickedness, and not there. Others, however, desire and ask the opposite:
that they may be allowed to enjoy themselves here, and that there he may do as he wishes—the founder of the great city, the judge of all the ages, and the ruler and Lord of humanity.
To him, together with silence, belongs all pure and glorious praise. Amen. Another, his second, by the same author, on [?].
On God's discipline, and a demonstration of whether the soul separates from the body without God's command, and on the kinds of death.
Again, then, as we praise the providence that watches over all things, and rely upon it as upon a wall beautifully fitted together from adamant,
and offer a demonstration in its defense to the best of our ability, we say these things to strengthen the clear understanding of simple people.
So that they may turn away from the many branches of falsehood and be led along the paths of truth. Let our wording, then, make clear what is necessary.
For if a composition is to be entrusted to things worked out by others, the thought is [?] and burdensome.
And the discourse is despised and discarded because there is a glut of it. We ourselves are caught in the conceit of loving [?] honor, since we plunder other people's treasures.
Let our composition, then, be clear or polished from the outset, so that, because of the [?] obscurity of what is translated,
that pasture [?] may not be swept into concealment [?] by my error, nor, because of the [?] meanness of what is said, may contemplation turn aside into foolishness.
For it is fitting that contemplation, when beautifully [?], should, like a bride splendid in color or in a mantle,
be wrapped in words. At the same time, let us also do this with care and a love of hard work: let us strengthen and confirm the discourse itself through the judgments of the Fathers,
so that we may not be thought to proceed differently, or according to a foundation laid by people who received illumination in the truth through the Spirit from above.
For every piece of writing or composition deprived of the things just mentioned is barren and bare.
It is rather foam, and brings no benefit at all to those who understand its meaning. But if it possesses some of these things and is bare of others,
it has only half the capacity to benefit and to be valued. I have said these things while, concerning the care that encompasses everyone,
I have an ocean in my heart. From it I also draw strength and help, as, for its sake, I try to offer these epigrams to many.
Every trial and every chastisement that rules over the world through the compassion of the righteous Father—we know that it happens for four [?].
For it is either to test [?], as in the case of good people, or for destruction and obliteration, or again to acquire [?], as in the case of [?] and wrongdoers—and for wrongdoers, doubly so.
Either to rebuke present evil, or to restrain future evil—in a threefold division—or to cleanse what is past.
Even a righteous person may be tried to cleanse some small stain; or discipline teaches him not to sin.
These things will be taught in other parts of the section. But the rod that hangs over this person has a single purpose, as the discourse has explained.
I mean testing and examination. These, then, have four forms: they come either from outside or from within one's household.
For the good law of providence, exercising discipline compassionately, first turns to outward things and admonishes owners through their possessions.
Then, if the admonition bears fruit, it lays the rod to rest, restrains itself, and holds back chastisement. But if not,
it begins with things within the household and belonging to the person himself. In the former case, it kills livestock, destroys crops, or strips lush orchards,
and does other things of this kind. In the latter case, it turns to the body, the soul, and the children: to the body through illnesses, and to souls through madness and possession,
and to the fruit of the womb through death and loss. And if evil is alarmed and grows quiet before the strength of the arm of discipline,
and long-standing sin is vomited out and dislodged, then the uplifted arm comes to rest, and the life-giving right hand shelters him.
But if not, the Lover of humanity comes through other, far more terrible things. He yokes him to slavery and leaves him in the hands of enemies.
And in the end he brandishes the sickle of destruction against him. Moreover, the hands of enemies and adversaries are a mighty rod. We know this also from those outside our faith.
But perhaps someone may ask whether God wills that a person should be put to death at the hands of enemies. And if he does not will it, why
does the defilement of murder run rampant among so many? But if he does will it, why does he crush and torment the murderer, either here or hereafter?
To these questions I will give this answer: in order that evil may be corrected, God sometimes takes care that this should happen,
handing the wicked person over to the murderer's destructive hand. At other times, however, he does not actually hand him over in the strict sense of the word, but rather withdraws his protection.
And so that this may become clear to us, let us briefly explain what handing over and abandonment are.

For we call it handing over when something is arranged through the help and assistance of God's all-wise hand, and provision is made for someone, according to his condition, to suffer at another's hands.
Withdrawal of protection, which we commonly call abandonment, is itself another kind of providential care.
This happens either when he does not forcibly restrain the freedom of the person intent on doing harm, although help is provided to the sufferer, or when he permits and allows this to happen.
And so that the meaning of what has been said may shine out more clearly and become [?], let us take the example of an emperor and a certain city under his rule.
He takes care of it in two ways: first, through the establishment of laws, military administration, and assistance
from his own hand, if it is attacked by a foreign power. But afterward, if that city gains no benefit from this,
and because of its great prosperity despises and scorns its ruler, he takes care of it in another way. If it is battered [?]
and attacked by a barbarian force, he leaves it to have its weaknesses exposed and deprives it of the help of his hand.
He orders the commanders to withdraw from it, so that through distress and war he may teach the wretched city how great a blessing peace is.
With this purpose, then, the great King and Lord of all is accustomed to instruct and care for the city—that is, our soul.
For when, despite his many acts of help, we do not train ourselves in virtue, he hands us over, withdraws his protection, and leaves and abandons us in the hands of enemies.
We will show from the holy writings that this is so. For when the prophet says concerning Jerusalem that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came against it,
and that the Lord handed it over into his hands, we understand his handing over the city to mean that he himself brought about the city's destruction,
and that the wicked Nebuchadnezzar served as an instrument, like a saw or an axe, for the destruction of the unjust city.
As another prophet declares: “I myself am rousing them, and I myself am bringing them. They will neither slumber nor sleep, nor will the straps of their sandals break,
as they come against you, daughter of my people,” and other such things. Through such words he leads us to understand that the city was being captured through the help and assistance of his hand.
This, then, concerns what handing over is. Withdrawal of protection, however, is illustrated by the expression Paul uses
when he says concerning wicked people, “God handed them over to a worthless mind,” and, “God handed them over to shameful passions,”
and, “For this reason God handed them over to the impure desires of their hearts.” In these passages he used “handed over” in place of “withdrew his protection and allowed.” For it is not just
that we acknowledge that this happened with his help and assistance, according to the first meaning of handing over.

Similar to this is what Moses, the leader of the Hebrews, said about a killer: “If he did not lie in wait for him, but God delivered him into his hands, I will make a place for you to which he may flee.”
The third meaning of handing over—for this alone remains for us to investigate—is like the case of Job. For God said to the accuser, “Look, he is handed over into your hands.”
This meaning is that of permission. For, as we showed above, handing someone over by helping is different
from handing someone over by standing aside and not rescuing or helping the person being killed; and different again is standing aside by permitting this to happen.
Now that these distinctions have been made, let us return to the question previously set before us.
If he wills it, he is [?] in the murderer’s deed. But if not, why does he stand aside and let this happen?
But if he wills it, why does he hold this man accountable through a sentence of judgment, either here or in the world to come? For we say that an action is judged according to the intention.
If the person who killed intended by this to fulfill God’s pleasure, he is to be praised to a very great degree.
An example of this is blessed Samuel, who cut the wicked [?] to pieces, and Elijah also, who slaughtered the false prophets and destroyed them through the zeal of his knife.
His sacrifice was priestly in every respect, and the Lord himself took great pleasure in it.
For he slaughtered priests who were murderers, and therefore we believe that he also received a reward for his intention and his slaughter.
But if the killer’s base intention has this purpose—to quiet the furnace of his anger and therefore rush toward destruction by the knife,
and stain his hands with the lawlessness of murder—the Lord, who loves humanity, certainly neither wills nor approves of this.
Nevertheless, he stands aside and allows it, and does not prevent this from happening, either cutting off wickedness together with life,
as in the case of sinners, or crowning and exalting virtue, as in the case of the righteous. He does indeed take pleasure in the person who is killed, but he certainly does not approve of the person
who kills. Although there are two persons, one who acts and another who suffers, the Just One is greatly incensed against the one who acts.
But in the one who suffers, his will is fully accomplished. That those who kill do not have it in their hearts
to please the one who lives forever, let us establish from the law, which says, “You shall not commit adultery, and you shall not murder,” and, “[?] by human hands his blood shall be shed.”

And at the same time, those who shed innocent blood. These others, however, were offered in sacrifice at the tyrant’s hands because they did not offer incense or worship a carved image in defiance of the Lord.
The Lord showed that the offering of their blood was acceptable, even though the hand of the priest was full of defilement.
Consequently, the punishments of persecutors are measured according to their intentions. “Let this be so,” someone says, “concerning those who shed innocent blood.
But what will you say about those who killed murderers and people known for other kinds of wrongdoing?
Did not these people also fulfill God’s pleasure?” That they fulfilled God’s pleasure, I too affirm and do not deny.
But this was not their aim. An example of this is that one of the kings of our own day went into battle, encountered one of his enemies, and struck him with his spear.
And he hurled a spear at him. Yet, contrary to his intention, it happened to strike him where he had an abscess.
When this burst open, the king found relief from his pain. The other man, however, had been intent on striking the king and killing him.

But the man who suffered the blow obtained what he had wholeheartedly desired. Although the deed was one and the same, because of the impulse of the will, the one was recognized as a murderer, while the other became healthy.
Something similar happened to a certain beggar, as we learned not long ago. This man was blind.
And a certain young man was playing in the city's open spaces with a ball made from dead animals' skins,
and struck him hard on his pupils, when the man happened by chance to be walking directly into the path of the ball.
Blood spurted from his eyes, and light entered his sight. The young man proved to be a physician, and the dead thing a light, even though he did not
intend it. Here too, although the action was a single one, the intentions of the two men—the one who acted and the one who suffered—were very different and far apart.
For that young man intended to prevail over his companions, while unknowingly sending the ball beyond the boundaries,
not to make a spring of light flow through the open, unprotected windows. The other man, however, was on an errand, perhaps to reach his destination, not to benefit from a blow.
Something like this also applies to the hateful deed that a murderer dares to inflict on his victim. For although the action itself is one and the same,
consider how far apart and different are the will of God and that of the killer. For the latter has this purpose:
by slaughtering the other man, to gain a little relief from the violence of his anger, as we mentioned above. God's purpose, however, is
that this man, on departing from life, should first of all gain some benefit. For this reason he either hands him over, leaves him unprotected, or permits this to be accomplished.
The murderer himself does not know that he has raised his neck against the Lord Almighty, although he is convicted by the judgment of his conscience. And therefore, from all these things...
It will therefore help us to examine in our discussion how many kinds of loss of human life there are, and what they are,
and whether a person departs from life at all without the command of the one who bound the soul together with the body.
So that our discussion may proceed and advance in an orderly way, let it first turn to the loss of life.
The loss of human life, then, sometimes comes about through God's decree, and sometimes through nature,
and also through free choice and through chance. As for that which comes through a decree, some occurs without an intervening cause, and some with a cause.
Of that which occurs with a cause, some belongs to the category of providential care and handing over, and some to that of withdrawal of protection and abandonment.
By losses of life without an intervening cause, then, we mean those brought about through fierce and merciless angels, who sharply and violently divide and separate

the union of soul and body. Such are those who are taken away while telling lies, crying out, or belching, or are forcibly led into the private chamber. By those involving a cause and providential care, however, we mean
widespread deaths, through which the Good One wipes out many, while the Just One causes particular individuals to flourish and preserves them.
Such are earthquakes and tremors of the earth, and destructive disturbances in the air, which wipe out the surrounding [?].
And scourges and torrents of fire, which sometimes come from the ether, sometimes are belched out by the depths, and sometimes arise in the clouds.
For these things and others like them are brought upon the world through the providence of the one who holds its reins, as he cleanses the house that its inhabitants have defiled.
You have evidence of these things both in Scripture and among the elderly who remember ancient events, and perhaps also through direct observation.
Then again, those whose lives come to an end through abandonment include those who are battered and strangled by cruel demons,
or are unjustly killed by an enemy, or perish through beasts that devour living creatures,
or are bitten and tormented by fiery serpents and venom-spitting creatures, or perish from eating deadly plants.
For these things and others like them do not happen through the providence and assistance of the one who rules the world.
Rather, when they occur, he leaves them alone and allows this to happen without preventing it.

It is clear, however, that when he foresees the benefit that will come from their departure, he withdraws the shade of his hand and the shelter of his right hand from those whose lives are being battered and cut short.
For if he had not withdrawn it, neither demon nor lion, neither enemy nor serpent nor poison would have harmed anyone or driven anyone out of life.
I began the discussion with these losses of life, which occur as though by a judicial sentence.
But death that occurs naturally is also divided into other categories. More precisely, these are two.
For a person dies either because of an imbalance or because of decline and weakness. This imbalance, through the increase and predominance of one of the elements [?],
arises in the body: either when the blood boils up and suffocates through its excessive quantity, or when the fiery bile increases
and torments the body with heat and drives the soul out of it, or when the bitter element boils up and, through another injury, [?] life.
There are also other conditions like these, through which a person departs this life.
For when this occurs, it destroys life in people of every constitution and every degree of strength. But the end also comes through decline and exhaustion, as it does for the elderly.
For although these people are free from imbalance, nevertheless, because their senses have grown dull and their strength has already sunk into weakness,
and the organs of their bodies have grown feeble, they pass within the barrier of death’s teeth peacefully and at the proper time, like an ear of grain reaped in its season,
or a prized vineyard harvested on its appointed day. We—or most people—usually call this a peaceful death. It is more fitting that it should be called a natural death.
This is because the person has completed the course of his life, and no other cause has ruined and destroyed him. But those other deaths,
because they are bound up with particular causes, are dreaded and bitter, and are not entirely in keeping with nature. The death of the elderly, however, belongs properly to nature,
in accordance with the span allotted to each living creature: one lives three hundred years, another thirty, and another three, or spans close to these or far different from them.
Someone might say that even the passing away of the elderly in this way is itself a kind of imbalance, because of an increase and rise in [?].
But this same end does not come upon them all. For we see many who have died silently and quietly.
When neither sickness nor pain had come upon them, nor had that sentence, as usual, shaken and convulsed their jaws and nostrils, but they simply faded and languished,
like a house that has grown old and falls without pressure or disturbance. So much, then, for the kinds of death that occur by a judicial sentence and those that occur naturally.
It remains for us to bring to light that other pair as well: those whose dissolution arises from the [?] of freedom, or, as it were, from
an accident or a chance occurrence. Those whose dissolution follows from freedom and the exercise of their own authority fall into two groups.
The first are like those in graves, in which many are sent to Sheol, both the weak and the vigorous.
As we have established concerning the wars of Ilium and Jerusalem and of other kingdoms, these wars came about because
freedom of choice summons and assembles people, stirs them up, and brings about death. The second are like those in taverns and [?].
For look: some young men in a certain place, heated with wine because they had drunk excessively and without restraint, slashed one another with knives.
Others hired a young woman, and after they had become senseless from wine, and anger had mixed with the wine, they paid her a miserable wage: slaughter by the knife.
Freedom did these things when it behaved foolishly in exercising its power. Another, third kind of death brought about by freedom
is the destruction of thieves and robbers: when they are caught in a raid, the judge’s sword slaughters them.

Or when these men encountered a company of merchants, and the merchants fought for their lives, they overpowered the robbers and made them dwell in the [?] of Sheol. Such are the deaths that arise from freedom.
Those that arise from accident and chance also have many variations. In the first kind, as we have seen happen to some people, a sling is aimed at a bird,
or a bow at a target or a moving animal, and someone happens to come into the path of the stone or arrow, is wounded or tormented, and meets his end as a result.
Likewise, someone riding may be thrown by the violent motion of his horse, and his life may depart with his fall.
Or again, someone walking may strike an old [?], stumble, and lose his life.
Or someone may be lying in a deep sleep and be frightened by some vision; when he jumps up and stands, he may slip from the roof or come upon a pit and fall into it.
We have examined these, and any other kinds that are hidden from us for the moment, and have found that death comes about through them.
Some, however, have defined this fourfold division as threefold: a blow from above, an act of free choice, and what happens naturally.
They have not considered what happens by chance worthy of mention at all. They draw support from the words of David the harpist, who said concerning Saul’s evil rule:
“Either his day will come and he will die, or the Lord will strike him and he will die, or he will be struck in battle and die.” They do not understand that the psalmist’s concern here
was not to speak about the kinds of death or the causes that bring about death, but rather to distance himself from responsibility for Saul’s destruction. Because of this expression, then,
many have come to a godless opinion, saying that only through a blow inflicted in anger does God take the soul from the body,
but not in these other cases. They turn against us and say this, arguing with weapons drawn from our own household:
“When a compelling force overcomes the body, whether from the impact of a sword, or from the force of a destructive poison, or from weakness and decay,”
As for the view which maintains that, in old age, punishment comes upon [?] without the command of the one who bound him, we say this in response:
Those who maintain this are guilty of a twofold error. First, this is clear from the words of the sacred psalmist,
who proclaims: “You take away their spirit, and they die and return to their dust.” For if, as they say, a person does not leave life by command,
then clearly this statement is false: “You take away their spirit, and they die.” In another place, too, the sacred word says:
“The Lord of lords does not take a soul away unless he has first devised a plan.” Next, there is also what we see happening every day.
For there are many whose bodies have been grievously tortured by sword wounds, yet they have not died.
Others, however, have been only slightly hurt by a blow, whether from a chastiser [?] or from a judge’s rod,
and have departed from life, because this was the will of the one who received them. Others he has taken while they were sleeping, and there are
those whom he has taken while they were talking. And why, indeed, do we see those who have undergone every kind of torture escape from the jaws of death,

while destruction comes upon others who are entirely at ease, unless the dwelling of the former is held firm by the command of the one who constructed it, while that of the latter is uprooted and loosened?
For according to the necessity and compulsion that affect bodies, those who have been slashed by countless swords ought not to live,
and those who were at ease in these circumstances ought not to be dissolved. Rather, it is the law of providence, accomplishing what is good and beneficial,
that determines when to help and whom it is fitting to lay low and deprive of life, whether an effective cause has already been put in place or not. By these considerations, the empty
and wretched objection already mentioned is done away with. And those who have established a threefold division for us, saying that the loss of life occurs
