either as punishment, through free will, or by nature—what will they say when they read of these things that happen by accident?
For there are those who were killed by an axe that slipped loose, as we read in Moses. There was no natural impulse against the victim, nor any act of free will.
For, it says, “He had not hated him previously.” Nor, indeed, was it a matter of punishment,
for the Lord did not strike him. It remains, then, for that fourth category to apply: that this departure from life occurs through abandonment and [?].
What benefits a person in the elevation [?] of life coincided and occurred together with destruction through the axe,
in the case of the man who suffered: by the word of the one who holds him, his soul was gathered away from him, and the loom of his life was broken.
But as for this notion which says that a person’s departure from life occurs apart from God’s law, it slips into profound error.
What need is there even to say that this makes the event a matter of disorder rather than care? And as we have said elsewhere,
it is therefore helpful to observe moderation, which is very beneficial to those who love what is profitable, and bring the course of our discourse to rest here,
while to the one who lives forever, the pilot of our lives and Lord of all, with the silence of speech we offer a tribute
of thanksgiving together with the gift of all praise—to him to whom glory unrestrained by silence is fitting.
Third discourse, on the same subject: the limit of human life and who determines it.
We approach a third contest concerning this, standing in argument before the one who has authority over our lives. We do not presume to investigate,
but explain what it is as far as we are able. We trust that we will not be put to shame, since we are not proceeding outside the proper aim.
Here too, let our discourse be complete, not deficient, and measured, not sprawling.
For if it sprawls and extends without measure, it causes distraction in the mind and weariness in the understanding,
and brings contempt upon its author. Just as sailors have a harbor, workers have rest, and travelers have a stopping place,
so an understanding that has labored and exercised itself in contemplation needs quiet and a respite from discourse. So much for this.
Let the discourse now return to its aim. We are examining whether our human lives
are bound by some definite, measured term, and whether it has been firmly decided from the beginning how long we are to remain alive, by the good law of providence—
or rather, by the one who has authority over our lives. For many people ask and investigate whether someone who departs this life,
whether by strangling, slaughter, or illness, necessarily had to depart from life here, at this time, and in this manner, and could not have lived any longer.
We give an answer to this, drawing upon the thoughts of the Fathers.
We arrange these at the end of our discussion [?], like a seal, a crown, and a protection—for a purse, a head, a house, and a city.
Thus it will not be plundered or treated with contempt, nor be attacked by tales. For the present, however, we will give an answer through our own reasoning,
first making this declaration: human lives have definite, known limits, and the time when they are shaken and taken away is determined.
But as for their ending in this manner or that—I mean through various causes that bring about their departure—
we will not discuss that yet. We demonstrate from the following that lives are determined and bounded by a certain appointed time. What do you say, my friend? Is it determined
and known to God when the life of each of us will enter the world, and when—and whether—this will happen? For example, that Noah should be in a certain generation,
and Abraham in another, and Moses likewise: yes or no? But if it is neither determined nor known, then the event is a matter of chance, not of care.
And the joining of the soul with the body would not take place according to reason or from reason, but according to the tales of those many people who say
that this is a principle of nature: whenever the womb suitably receives the seed deposited in it, the soul is immediately brought into being and created there by God.
This is largely unworthy of belief. For it is acknowledged that one has greater suitability than another
for [?] and for giving birth. Yet the Good One has often restrained that suitability,
and likewise overcome the lack of suitability. Scripture also demonstrates this in what it tells us about the wombs of barren women.
At the same time, nature itself teaches us that, conversely, fruitfulness occurs when seed is deposited.
And he, the Good One, sends the soul on its journey together with the body, as is fitting and when it is fitting, whether there is benefit or not.
We know that this also happened with the world. For its Maker, though he had intended from eternity to create it, brought it into being together with time,
and dissolves it together with time, for a reason and as is fitting—that is, within determined limits. He who holds its limits transcends the beginning and end of the world.
Therefore Gregory, that foremost master, says: “You who make everything and then change it again by your skillful word,
at the time and moment you know to be fitting, in the depth of your wisdom and providence.” In this way, then, we must also understand our human lives.
For the time of our entry into the world is appointed and determined by God. Likewise, the time of our departure is measured and determined.
But perhaps one of those who delight in disputes will raise an objection against me, saying this: “If someone had not left his house at that hour,
and had not undertaken a journey along the [?] road, he would have escaped the murderer’s attack. And if he had not rashly attempted to cross the river,
boldly confronting the force of its current, he would not have drowned.
“So, then, the thread of his life could have been extended further, and it is not determined by some appointed time.”
Let us offer the following refutation of this wretched thought, with Scripture first administering its rebuke: “What answer do you give me about this, you there?
“And Job’s sons and daughters—if they had not been under the roof of their eldest brother’s house, even if they had not been destroyed by the collapse of the house,
would they not have perished in some other way?” And this fire destroyed the shepherds, as the account relates. We must think in this way also about the destruction of large numbers of people.
For just as there the sword destroyed together both the young people who loved companionship and pleasures and the [?] in the open country and the enclosures,
so the appointed moment of death overtakes us when we complete the allotted span of life, and [?] from life is beneficial.
Furthermore, we also have a certain account of something that happened shortly before our time.
A young man was crossing the River Tigris near the city of the Assyrians, passing over a bridge built of boats.
A peasant driving a horse came toward him and, in his rush, knocked the young man aside and plunged him into the river.
The young man’s wretched fall was seen by many men standing beside the river.
They ran and secured the saving of his life. Not long afterward, however, he came to a drinking house and was celebrating his deliverance and rescue in the company of many people,
drinking merrily. As evening drew near, he came to the table; then, befuddled by both wine and sleep, he stumbled on the roof and struck the earth, his mother,
and lay in the [?] of Sheol. Experience itself also refutes these things. For we know many who entered battle and received countless sword blows,
and were battered by spear thrusts and volleys of flying arrows, yet, when they returned and came back from battle, received medical treatment but did not escape the teeth of death.
There are others, however, into whose very lives the sword had penetrated, and who had already been counted among the dead, but when the physicians—the veterinarians who
accompany the army—came and found them still breathing, they restored them to health by extracting the projectile. This very thing happened.
There was also a man among the profit-loving merchants. While he was traveling east with a large company, robbers overtook them, and they clashed with one another in battle.
Those wicked men sent most of his companions to the grave. They also struck him violently with a sword on his tender neck, and he was counted among the dead.
A day later, when some villagers were searching among the dead, they found him still breathing.
They picked him up and carried him away from there, and through the efforts of physicians they greatly strengthened his weakened life.
He lived for fifty years after that. “Yes indeed,” says the opponent, “you have certainly strengthened our argument!
For here, while he was drawing further breaths, he was granted the chance to live in [?] manner.
What else happened, except that the one who measures out life can extend its limit? Hezekiah is a sign of this.
After he received the sentence, ‘You will die and will not live,’ fifteen years were subsequently added to his life.” But I, my good man, say this, and I do not reach my conclusion rashly:
If the appointed end of that man's life had not been set and determined for a later time, he would have been crushed there, together with all his other companions, by the [?] that brings departure.
But because the fabric of his life still had to be stretched out further, it was not cut short then.
Although the cause was pressing, the Good One brought it to nothing, procuring for him the benefit that would come from life.
But perhaps you argue differently and declare categorically that there is no fixed measure for our lives.
And, like an excellent athlete, you have confronted the adversary with his own weapons. Answer me, then, as I ask a small question.
Does God's knowledge know what is beneficial and what is going to happen—yes or no? But if it does know,
and knows these things precisely, and knows, wills, and brings about what is beneficial, it must also bring human lives to an end at a definite point,
seeing what is beneficial in their departure. There are four things: knowledge, action, the limit of life, and what is beneficial in the ending of lives.
As for action accompanying knowledge, we do not recognize this in God in every case, but only where it is beneficial. How so?
For as the source of all wisdom, he knows all the shameful things that human beings have done or are doing. Yet he never assists or helps with these.
But he does act when he knows what is beneficial, as it is said in the Gospel: “My Father is working until now, and I too am working.”
That is, for the continuance and preservation of existing things. For example, that the sun should rise, that plants should sprout again, and that animals should give birth to living young.

And, above all, that we should receive immortality through death, because of the succession that springs up through birth. But since we have said that the Good One does not bring about everything he knows,
for the sake of consistency let us mention this too, even if we stray somewhat from our subject. For we say that he does not do everything he can,
nor everything he wills. For he wills that we should not turn aside from the holy commandments, nor stain our hands with murder,
nor defile our bodies with the shamefulness of sexual immorality. Although he wills these things, he never undertakes to make us refrain from them by force.
Let us also recognize that he has the power to make countless worlds and is able to create wings for human beings to fly with.
And flaming wings, and eyes on his feet, and [?] on his chest. Yet he does not do this merely because he knows how and is able.
But let my argument turn and proceed toward its goal. If God knows our departure and our [?] from here as something determined,
and, knowing it, brings it about because he judges this better, then human lives are indeed determined and measured out.
But if this is true, those who say that our lives are something unfixed should change their words: that they contract and expand, going back and forth like wood on water,
and drift and float without being known or determined, and are like a ship without a pilot, without beginning or end. “But,” someone says, “God is not bound by a limit,
and if he wishes, he lengthens life, and if he wishes, he shortens it. And who is it who brings God under the yoke of necessity
and limitation?” Or perhaps you suppose that a limit exists for the sake of harmony and good order. But if this is what you think, you are very much mistaken,
and you are driving the truth away from yourself. For God, who established order among existing things, is not a God of disorder and confusion.
But if you use “limit” to mean something coercive and tyrannical, by which God is constrained as he sets limits to our lives, this is something rejected and dismissed
by our thinking and our argument. For we believe in God, and we acknowledge that he knows necessary things as possibilities,
and determined things without being determined himself, and things subject to a limit without being limited himself.
He is under no necessity, as we are, to be confined within the pressures of possibilities and necessities, or to understand knowable things according to the way we know them,
either uncertainly or distinctly. For example, we know in a definite way those things that occur by nature,
such as that the sun is bright, the earth solid, the wind moving, and the soul alive. We distinctly know this particular property given to nature,
which people skilled in words call “necessity.” But things that are not bound by nature we know uncertainly,
such as whether or not we will have rain tomorrow, or whether or not we will enter into partnership or friendship. These they call possibilities.
In the same way, we apprehend things that are contained and confined within a spatial limit by a conception that envisages a spatial limit.
And our material nature, which is limited to a body, cannot conceive them through a thought that is unlimited.
But does the wondrous God possess these things, as I said, in a way beyond us or in the same way as we do, both in power and in wisdom?
Therefore he is not bound under necessity and limitation either. And although his own might is exalted above these things, he has subjected us and our lives
to limitation and to the necessity of a beginning and an end, so that we should not become contemptible and despised, or estrange ourselves and wander away from the order
that has been bound up with created things and has run its course with them from the beginning. For it would be absurd if,
while he established a limit for night and day, and measured out for all living creatures, according to their seasons, birth and growth, habitation and nourishment,
so that even the crane and the swallow know the time of their arrival, as Scripture says, we should remain ignorant of these things and be left out.
But if you are pleading God's case, and it grieves him to have his dominion diminished, and you tell me deceitfully that, if he wishes, he lengthens life:
And if he wishes to shorten life, I too accept this, and I send up a sigh mixed with lamentation over those who are sick in this way.
And I also say that, if he wishes, he shortens life, adding that he does so if shortening it is beneficial.
And I say that, if he wishes, he lengthens life, knowing—and it does not escape him—where life's end lies and when it is beneficial not to depart from it.
And again I say that, if he wishes, he lengthens life, and he is able and has the authority to accomplish this.
But he does not wish to do so, judging according to what is advantageous and more beneficial for a human being. For the statement that says, “If he wishes, he lengthens life,
and if he wishes, he shortens it,” establishes for us God's inviolable sovereignty and almighty power. Thus this principle is adopted at the outset:
if he wishes, he does this, and if he wishes, that. Yet he directs the impulse of his activity toward what is advantageous.
For this reason he rightly threatened Hezekiah, the king of the Israelites, with the removal of his life through the message of Isaiah, without being unaware of the end of his life.

And he prophesied to him, “You are dying, and you will not live.” If, indeed, this had been the proper end and limit of the king's life here, and it had not been beneficial for him to live any longer,

but rather for him to depart and [?] prepare then for his departure, he would no longer have needed the prophet's announcement and the tears that followed it, together with instructions concerning his departure.
For Hezekiah knew that [?] the pain, and the bond of the illness afflicting his body was loosened, he should entrust instructions concerning his departure to his household.
Rather, the source of all help used such a statement so that he would not be overcome by the disease of pride,
as though it were because of his virtue that the power of the destroying angel had struck down the ranks of the Assyrians. Therefore, when the prophet [?] returned to him and announced to him
the doubling of the life already mentioned, he cried out and proclaimed in praise, “I said that at the height of my days I would depart.”
Those who are practiced in such interpretations say that the “height of days” is the height of prosperity that he attained
through righteous prayer, by which he laid low the legions of the Assyrians. But if someone reads, according to another version,
“I said that in the middle of my days I would depart,” even so, the meaning accords with the interpretation before us.

That is, the “middle of days” means that, when they have been measured out as either thirty or a hundred, they may afterward be cut short and reduced from that measure, like a [?] by a rope that draws it in and shortens it.
Thus these things make it clear and distinct to us that human lives are enclosed within a certain limit and measure, which we customarily call a fixed term, that is, an appointed time.
We do not attempt to say, like those who suffer from the disease of foolishness, that there is some decree, decision,
or limit imposed upon God, because of which he is entirely unable to shorten or lengthen the lives of earthly beings.
For who imposed this constraint upon him, so that he should keep the earliest inhabitants of the world alive for such and such a length of time,
but shorten the lives of others and measure them out at a hundred and eighty years, according to the limits given by David?
Rather, in avoiding this, we draw near to what accords with true reverence for God.
And to avoid confusion, we say that the Good One has given us a limit to life according to the judgments of his providence.
While he guides us toward what greatly benefits us in the course of these troubled and impoverished lives.
And he acts according to the immeasurable greatness of his wisdom, which made the worlds, both in bringing us into life and in taking us out of life.
At the time and moment when he knows it is beneficial, he does not leave nature to wander about on its own and go wherever it wishes, like a horse rushing headlong,
or like the movement and outpouring of the restless wind [?]. Above all, it is without understanding and without reason even to comprehend it.
But when they abandon these propositions laid down earlier and contend with the truth and with us, they also take the saying of Jeremiah, that compassionate man among the prophets,
and bring it forward before us, turning to what God said when declaring: “If I speak concerning a nation and a kingdom, to uproot and to tear down,
to overthrow and to destroy, and that nation turns from its wickedness, I too will turn from what I intended against them.”
“A saying like this,” they say, “does not subject God to the compulsion of necessity.” But to those who mutter these things,
we will gladly say this: “We do not bring God under the yoke of necessity, you people! He is not under necessity.
For we are not so completely bereft of perception and understanding that we would bend under compulsion and subject to necessity the one who is above every power and dominion.
For no obligation has been imposed on him to measure out our lives in this way, according to a prescribed number,
so that the course of his work should be completed from morning to evening. Rather, as the treasury of all understanding, he has measured and determined our lives through foreknowledge,
which proceeds to action at the proper time: how long it benefits us to dwell in bodily life, and when it is advantageous for us to be cut off from it.
And if we do not accept this as true—that God is master of both, namely, of binding us and releasing us, and that the time of each is distinctly known to him and kept by him—
then we must necessarily admit that our affairs are tossed about in confusion and turmoil, and that they proceed and are governed apart from God.
But so that I do not make the saying of that compassionate one a stumbling block, I will clarify this for you, lest an untrained understanding bewilder you and cause you great harm.
Such, in its bare form, is the word of God. For that treasury of benefits is accustomed to use the form of a threat to bring about a change,
and to put on the appearance of someone who is angry, although his eagerness is directed toward what is beneficial. Thus, also to the Ninevites,
through Jonah the seer, he foretold the overthrow of their city, while giving those wicked people an opportunity for repentance and salvation.

It was not that he did not know whether they would repent or not, and whether deliverance or destruction would consequently follow for them. Rather, that power which surpasses all reckoning was arranging this:
that when they heard the threat, they would refrain from evil and repent, and would not suffer the things threatened.
But if this had not been his desire, it would have been very easy for him to crush them with manifest destruction.
Nor would he have needed the [?] of the fugitive prophet, which happened to them a little later. For when, after a considerable time, from the fruits of their grievous deeds
they had grown distant, they returned to their wickedness. And in the days of Nahum they received the judgment they deserved, without a prophet being sent.
For they had quickly forgotten the patience and kindness of God that they had learned [?].
And no other preacher was needed to admonish them. Yet perhaps, in their foolishness and frivolity, they were saying, “What have the words of the son of Amittai come to?”
For just as a cloud of darkness had concealed his words, so they were thinking about the words of another preacher as well.
And so they became the agents of their own complete destruction. He had indeed sent beforehand, and through Jonah he had disciplined and threatened them,
without forgetting or mistaking the appointed time of punishment and that end which would come upon them without fail. And in the days of Nahum he carried them away.
Rather, his purpose was that, through words of threat and warning, he might turn back the many in whom there was a leaven of virtue,
bring them back from the errors of wickedness, and grant them deliverance from judgment.
It is like a thoughtful man of great understanding, an instructor and teacher of many groups, both foolish and intelligent:
he corrects the former with the force of his hands and his whip, and, remaining mute and entirely silent, subjects them to instruments of [?]. But the latter
he sets right through admonitory speech and urges toward virtue, which is taught to a free mind more effectively than by rods.
But if they gain no benefit even from the blow of a word, he judges them, to their misfortune, as he does the foolish. In the same way, God, the instructor of all,
strikes the foolish and wicked, who will not be corrected by words, with a rod of discipline. But for those
who conceive repentance through admonition, he brings it about through envoys and messengers.
Therefore he destroyed the deeply wicked people of Sodom in silence, through a severe judgment. For he knew that words would never bring them to an end of their wickedness.
For how could a messenger have benefited those who even made the angels sent for their destruction into an occasion for their own misfortune?
But those earlier inhabitants of Nineveh he disciplined through the word of a messenger sent to them,
and he turned many of them away from the errors of wickedness. In the end, however, they received the judgment of the people of Sodom, when their former practices had become ingrained.

And from opposing elements, which did not run together, they received a twofold sentence. For the river that flowed within their city and the fire that burst forth from the [?] of the wilderness—the former
swept clean the portion on the ground, while the latter consumed the portion in the air. History has taught us these things, as has the word of Nahum,
which cries out figuratively about their judgment. But perhaps someone will say that God is false, since he promised this or that and did not do what he had agreed to do.
In answer to this we offer an illustration from education. Suppose an instructor says to a boy, “I will flog you and strike you,”
and makes other bitter words ring in his ears, while intending and aiming at this: that through warning and fear the boy’s education should advance,
and that there should be no need for force from his hand or for blows. Do we then say that the instructor lied because he promised the boy that he would strike him but did not? Certainly not,
if we consider his aim and intention, which is that, by whatever means, the boy should be trained in the subjects he is learning.
He ought, indeed, to have made his wording conditional: “I will strike you if you are negligent in your reading.”
But the threat, “I will strike you,” is sufficient to make the boy understand that the instructor’s threatening words concern his negligence.
There was no need to state it with a qualification, but rather to use it in that sense. The following also belongs to the same kind:
the word that the Merciful One addressed to the Assyrian people: “Forty days from now, Nineveh will be overthrown.”
That is, if they do not repent. Since this is the intention of the wording, we say that he did not lie.
For if he had said, “Forty days from now, Nineveh will certainly be overthrown,” but afterward, when it repented,
it could escape being overthrown, then perhaps the charge of falsehood would be justified. But in fact he made neither statement with an explicit qualification,
nor did he say that it would inevitably perish. Yet the outcome of the affair showed that the threatening word was sent and the pronouncement made so that they would repent:

that this city, Nineveh, would be destroyed [?] at such-and-such a time. The word of the blessed Jeremiah also has this meaning. For there the Lord spoke to him with an explicit qualification, saying:
“If I pronounce a word concerning this or that people, whether for harm or for good, and they turn and abandon their evil or good practices,
they will not experience what was intended.” This is not said as though the time of their destruction and the appointed end of their ruin were fixed absolutely and without qualification.
For he has defined and made clear that, when they treat that threatening word lightly and increase [?] and [?], he destroys them then and there.
But if they persist in it—and he knows this beforehand—even if he does not bring them to their end immediately, he nevertheless holds it all together in his foreknowledge.
This was clearly demonstrated by the Assyrian example that was cited. And why, it is asked, did Moses, the instructor in the law—or rather, the one who speaks through Moses—command
that we put parapets around roofs and place a covering over a pit? Was it not to free himself from responsibility for destructive and fatal death [?]?
He himself also said, “Let no one fall and then say, ‘This happened to me because of the Lord.’” Quite so; I too am not disputing this.
For I know that the Merciful and Just One has never been a cause of stumbling to anyone. He takes care not to be thought of in this way, and that an unjust suspicion
should not lead many to pass judgment on him on this account, when freedom was the cause of destruction through someone’s climbing up to the height of the roof.
If someone, dizzy and confused by sleep, should slip and fall, he might accuse God of being the cause. Through his command, therefore, he warns us to make parapets for roofs.
As we demonstrated in the discourse before this one, the kind of cause that brings about the loss of life is distinct from the cause of life’s appointed end and of death.
For God is not necessarily the cause of the former, as we demonstrated. But God is necessarily the cause of dissolution and departure [?], in every circumstance, as we have shown.
As for that saying of Moses, I have heard others interpret it as follows. This interpretation too is helpful and belongs in the present discussion.
For they say that the Hebrews had learned about fortune and fate through their association with the Egyptians: the former is something that
happens by accident and chance, whether evil or good; the latter is something brought about by the governance of the heavenly powers,
namely the wandering and non-wandering stars, determined and fixed, from which there is no escape. So that they should not be afflicted by disturbances through this madness and blaspheme,
either by saying that there is no providence, in accordance with the notion of fortune, or by transferring responsibility for evil and good, misery and prosperity, to God

rather than to the exercise of their own freedom, as they ought, he appropriately commanded them so that they would not suffer these things. He kept them away from foolish opinions, and these things from all this [?].
But let us turn away from this and give an answer to the frivolous thinker who disputes with us. “Look,” he says, “we see a weak man who charged at a division of cavalry.”
“And they consequently put an end to him. Had they not done this, perhaps he would not have died.”
Yet, my good man, have you never seen or heard of a mighty, strong, and confident man who boldly attacked some weak men, but met his end from a single blow?
I have heard of it, and I had no difficulty believing that someone who had been very successful in conflicts and battles was struck down by a weak man.
Perhaps the Good One was rebuking the lawlessly forceful arm of the mighty man who relied on his own strength.
We will make you our advocate, godly youth—you who used your sling and brought Goliath to a miserable death.
There are also people whose strength was evenly balanced, who grappled with one another in combat and crushed one another.
Sometimes a weak man kills a mighty man; and a mighty man, in turn, kills someone whose arm is weak, or another mighty man like himself.
Now if, according to the account just given, the weak man’s charge against the division brought about his death, it would follow
that the mighty man who escaped from the weak man’s hand should acknowledge that his release did not come from some other assault, independently of the word of the one who bound him.
And if the Lord of strength left the mighty man in the hands of the weak man, it is clear that he also strikes down the weak man through the hands of the mighty.
In the former case he overthrows the strength of sin; in the latter he corrects and disciplines a life spent in sin. In both cases he has in view what is beneficial.
But the foolish statement, “If so-and-so had not done that, he would not have stumbled into death,” deserves considerable ridicule.
For this same argument can be applied to anything. If someone did not eat too much, he would not become ill; and if he did not become overheated
or chilled, or suffer some other affliction, he would not endure the distress of illness
. But this foolish reasoning is refuted as follows: if someone did not eat, he would not even have the ability to move.
It is because he eats that he is able to move. And the sinner would not be put to death by a bitter blow if wickedness had not pleased him.
Nor would the first of our race, in the beginning, have been estranged from the tree of life and from Paradise if he had not tasted from the tree of knowledge.

But because the sinner delighted in his wickedness, and Adam found sweetness in the fruit and in trampling on salvation, the former was handed over to a destructive end, and the latter to miserable exile.

Therefore, because God knew beforehand [?] that, although the sinner could refrain from sin, he nevertheless chose it and carried it out—since, had he not sinned [?], he would not have been swallowed up by death—
because he took pleasure in it and sinned, God also determined and appointed his death as something beneficial. For the Good One knows what is possible without uncertainty,
just as he knows our freedom. In our own understanding, we reason that if someone had not entered a conflict or battle, he would not have been overtaken by his end.
And if another person had not entered a house whose walls were leaning, he would not have perished in the house when it collapsed. But God knows and sees beforehand
that, although the former could refrain from entering the battle, he is all the more determined to enter it, and that he will not escape being killed.
And, seeing this, he looks upon him with providential care. For he did not apprehend this merely as a possibility, since he knew it unalterably.
To the outcome and conclusion of the event, and not, as we rashly say, “If we do not [?], we do not [?].”
For if, because someone went beneath a roof resting on plastered walls and [?] and was killed, the very same thing ought to have happened to the others as well.
Yet we both see and hear that, in the very same house, while many were lying down, one, he says, escaped from the enclosure of death’s teeth,
while another met his end immediately. But, he says, he hid beneath a vine or a tree or something else,
and found escape as though by chance. Yet many died merely from fear of the house’s collapse, and those who investigate hidden things
were left bewildered and astonished, seeing an end that drove men out of life without suffering or injury. Others, however, were saved by
the Good One. Though they were violently thrown down from the height of the roof, they did not die. Another suffered only a small fall and immediately went to Sheol.
To others the Good One granted deliverance from drowning in deep waters and the surging force of rolling currents.
Paul’s ship confirms this: it laid all its [?] upon the outspread surface of the water,
and was itself shattered into many pieces. Yet we do not hear that any one of them was crushed by death. About others, however, we have received this report:
when their ship was broken apart by the waves, it cast out its men along with its cargo, and they all went into the prison of death’s teeth.
Such was the ship of Odysseus, which a storm shattered and [?]: it saved the resourceful man and drowned his companions, whose dealings were evil.
We have already discussed these things above. The discussion is therefore sufficient as it stands.
“And how,” they say, “did the appointed end of the dead man’s life coincide with the will of the murderer or of the person administering poison? It is astonishing,” they say.
Nor am I myself free from amazement in my mind, as I offer thanksgiving to the Lord and marvel greatly at the magnitude of what has happened.
But I say that, when it was helpful and greatly conducive to the salvation of the life of the man who was killed, and it was fitting for his release to occur here and in this way,
he brought about that release through the Lord’s action. The hidden hand hurried forward when it saw the visible hand, and delivered the man from life.
But if, in this case too, it had not been beneficial for him to leave this life, he would have restrained the destructive hand, as we have explained many times.
Likewise, if it had not been fitting for him to die in this way, through another form of assistance,
either forceful or compassionate, he would have guided him. But if he who holds the rudders of the world in his hand knew beforehand
that some cause—poison, fever, a rupture, or a fall—would strike this man, and left the rudders of his care unattended,
and did not bring about deliverance in this life, but judged his release from life according to what was beneficial, then to add to and magnify his judgment,
and to crown his judgment, is always our duty. So much for these matters. It is therefore appropriate, as we recall the discussion of what the appointed end is,
and distinguish it from chance and fate, that we conduct our discussion enlightened by the judgments of the fathers.

We find, then, that “end” is a term with several meanings, applied to many occurrences according to the context, as the words of the saints will make clear. In one place it is used in place of “boundary.”
In another sense, however, it refers to a blow and a chastising rod; sometimes to some cause; and elsewhere to declaration and knowledge.
And in another sense, to payment and amount [?]. For where Scripture says, praising God’s [?] providential care:
“He has set a limit to darkness, and he knows beyond the end,” it uses the word to mean a boundary. That is, [?] evening and darkness; the sun’s movement produces daytime.
For when the sun’s sphere runs beneath the earth’s shadow, God has established darkness there as the order of night.
Therefore the victorious man says, “He has set a limit to darkness,” meaning an order and boundaries.
Again, when he says, taking providence as his subject at the outset, “He makes fools of the wise and destroys the words of the innocent,
and he destroys the righteous and sinners alike,” and afterward adds, “All these are parts of his ways,” he uses “limit” in place of “cause,”
so that the wording would mean this: “Because of his ways—that is, his incomprehensible judgments—
he governs these things in this manner.” But Moses spoke of declaration when he said, as though speaking in the person of the Lord:
“The end of [?] flesh has come before me.” For here “end” is used to declare that he has pronounced judgment on them.
This is clear, because this “end” could not possibly be understood as indicating any of the other meanings.
But Habakkuk the seer used it to mean a blow and a chastising rod: “The end is coming and will not prove false.
And if it delays, do not kill yourselves.” As for payment and amount, Ezekiel and the trumpet of the Gospel use it. The former says, “He has not lent at interest,”
and the latter, “He agreed with some of his workers for a denarius a day.” For here “agreed” and “interest” are used with reference to payment.
Perhaps someone might also use the term “limit” for the boundary of life, considering David’s statement: “I have seen a limit to every end, but your commandment is very, very broad.”
We have therefore explained these things so that we may escape the trap of error.
Let us consider: when we apply the term “end” to death, in which of the meanings already mentioned is it being used?
[?] Is it in the sense of a judicial sentence, or in the sense of a boundary? For we regularly use these two meanings when discussing departure from life.
So much, then, concerning the end. Fate, however, is [?], from which to escape [?]. It opposes and destroys freedom,
and at the same time is entirely foreign to chance. Chance, in turn, is a certain impulse that proceeds spontaneously from rational or irrational beings,
or from animate or inanimate things, and comes about without any fixed bounds. It too, in turn, effaces and restricts authority over the household.
When, therefore, we say that human lives have boundaries and are determined and fixed by God, and that the end overtakes a person and comes upon him from God,
we certainly wish to remain far removed from these foolish and godless ideas: from the idea of chance, on the one hand,
by acknowledging that the order and measure of the beginning and end of our lives are fixed by the one who joined the soul to the body,
and who releases it at a suitable time [?], and again binds it inseparably at the proper time.
We avoid belief in fate, however, when we do not indiscriminately attribute to God, and charge him with, the causes of life and of departure from life.
For it is not fate that one person dies so miserably [?], while another departs in blessedness, but this comes from the one who weighs our deeds in the balance and judges them.
Even if he removes some people from life, either by handing them over or by allowing it, he himself does not bow to compulsion, nor does he wish to descend to the point of coercing our freedom.
For this reason he frequently makes use of permission, but only rarely and occasionally of handing people over.
For handing people over comes close to necessity, whereas permission accords with freedom,
allowing it and leaving it to turn wherever it pleases and as much as it wishes. For the present, let these remarks about fate and chance suffice.
Especially since, in the discourse that follows this one, you will, God permitting, be with us [?] and share our diligent inquiry.
Let us therefore introduce the [?] of the fathers, so that we may not be judged to be saying something foreign when we declare that human life has a limit.
We have made this clear. From Basil, from the discourse entitled “God Is Not the Cause of Evils.”
For he takes wealth away from those who use it, in order to destroy their instrument of wrongdoing.
He brings sickness upon those for whom it is beneficial to be bound in their limbs, or to have their impulses toward sin restrained.
Deaths are brought about when the limits of life are fulfilled—limits that God’s just judgment established from the beginning for each one of us,
having determined far in advance what is beneficial for each of us. And a little later:
Yet it was surely necessary to understand that, when people suffer from moderate and curable illnesses, they receive help through medical care.
But when the affliction proves beyond relief, it becomes necessary to cut away the part that has become corrupted,
so that the disease may not spread through its connection with the vital parts. From the Theologian, from the discourse on his brother Caesarius.
O governor and benefactor of our souls, you who made everything and transform and set everything in order through your skillful Word,
at the time and in the manner you know, in the depth of your wisdom and providence: receive Caesarius now as the firstfruits of our journey.
Whether another should come first, we leave to your decisions, on which everything depends in these matters. Receive us also afterward, at the proper time,
when you have guided us for as long as is beneficial. The Theologian did not state and reveal the limit of life as explicitly as the blessed Basil did.
But by saying, “At the time and in the manner you know,” and “Receive us at the proper time,” and “For as long as is beneficial,”

he gives us reason to understand that there is a beneficial limit [?], that we live for as long as is helpful, and that our departure and passing take place according to a certain measure and at the proper time.
From Saint Ephrem, from the discourse against Bardaisan. Because God foreknew the slain who would be killed by murderers, he set the limit of their lives at their killing.
Yet he is far removed from the wickedness of the murderer who dared to kill, and also far removed from the chance occurrence of the victim’s sudden killing. If, then, the slain person

departed before his appointed end, it is chance; and if he departed at his appointed end, it is a stumbling block. But God is exalted above both chance and stumbling. It is not chance when the appointed end draws near.
Nor is the judgment to come a stumbling block. Yet even though these things have already been explained, they still need explanation, for it is difficult to understand how

the hidden appointed end of the murdered person and the murderer’s will coincided at the same moment, so that the murdered person departed at his appointed end, while the murderer incurred condemnation.
Separating the body from the soul belongs to God the Creator; but separating the soul from the body also belongs to the person who longs for virtue.
And if anyone considers credible and authentic the book called the Ascents, whose authorship is the subject of dispute and disagreement on many people’s lips—
for some say that it is by Evagrius, others by Eusebius of Caesarea, by Macarius, the great one among the solitaries, or by Philoxenus of Mabbug—
we refer him to it. When he encounters its seventh discourse, entitled “On the Commandment of the Righteous,” let him rejoice to learn from it that we are not uttering [?].
Then there is David’s saying, “Look, you have given my days a measure,” and our Savior’s saying, “Are not two sparrows sold for two pennies?” and other sayings like these.
Since these are clear and more or less known to everyone, we pass over them. These, then, are the judgments of the fathers.
Let what remains be a prayer. For I pray and bend the knees of my heart.
For the learned, I pray that they may flee from defiled things and the love of contention, follow the plain truth, and not despise it because of its author’s weakness.
May they keep far from envy and heed the admonition of the blessed Ephrem, who earnestly entreats them and gives this advice:
“When the strong and the weak among the thirsty search for water, even if the weak happen to find the spring,
the strong also benefit with them and rejoice together. They do not hang back and hold themselves aloof because the weak found it, depriving themselves, out of envy, of relief from their thirst.

So too with those who investigate the truth: if it happens to be in a weak person’s hands, let it not be spat out because we are sick from the sting of envy.” But may God help me abundantly, and over me

may he spread the shelter of his grace, which surpasses understanding. In every way may he protect and rescue me from evil, and in every matter and every word establish me as a partner in the truth, one who fulfills and honors it.
May he grant me delight, both here and there, in his pure glory and through his exalted knowledge—to him for whom it is fitting to release praise from silence.
His fourth discourse, on the law of providence, on fortune and fate, and also on poverty and wealth.
By Antony of Tikrit, surnamed Gurgan. The fruit of toil is sweet. Labor [?] the discerning mind; it is the source of all good things.
One can find that the person who is lazy is tormented by every hardship amid his groaning. Those who see him subject him to every indignity and do not pity him when they see his misery.
But if a diligent person, after much toil, struggle, and weariness, receives a double yield of fruit and benefit, they honor and exalt him.
Along with his blessings, they also bestow praise on him. And if he does not succeed, but fails and is left without fruit,
they do not subject him to blame. Therefore I too, upon whom care and diligence are laid, and who am surrounded by unending toil,
so that I may declare God’s providence, which surpasses understanding, show how great it is and what it is like, and proclaim it without fault or blame—
it is fitting for me to direct the eyes of my mind toward the encouragement of the attentive and diligent, and to become like those who turn watercourses and dig wells,
who dive into the depths and search through mines for silver. For all these together, the deeper they probe,
All this brings fruit along with them, while springs gush forth in abundant streams.
And there are very many cold [?]; those engaged in mining find columns of silver through narrow shafts.
Divers who hold their lives cheap bring up precious stones from the depths. And, without wearying you, I recall the deeds prompted by a love of hard work,
and speak of the fruits that come from diligence. But I am straying from the aim set before me; I will return to the subject connected with our discussion.
As I look to its Father, I will approach the discourse with prayer, so that our discussion may proceed in an orderly sequence.
I will examine the teachings that encourage idleness and drag many into the abyss of evil. And, as though illuminating dark paths,
we will shed light on them through the word of truth and lead people who love God to turn away from them.
These are the matters concerning the terms fortune and fate that, as we agreed in the preceding discourse, we would take up at length.
I also include chance, coincidence, and encounter, and any other things resembling these.
Fate is a necessity from which there is no escape. The teaching about it is divided into two opinions.
Some say that it comes from the stars, while others derive it from God. Let us begin with the teaching of the pagans.
For they assigned the direction and governance of earthly affairs and of this whole universe to fate and the revolution of Olympus,
saying that the conjunction of the seven wandering lights with one of the twelve signs of the zodiac determines misfortune and suffering,
happiness and glory, birth and death, poverty and wealth, sickness and health, intelligence and stupidity,
and many other opposites, as well as actions arising from free will—I mean depravity and chastity,
compassion and ruthlessness. They say that these things are destined to occur by the one who allots them, and that there is no way to escape or evade them.
For example, when Zeus stands in a particular position, a man who will be a king will enter the world.
When the sun is in Leo, a vigorous man and a hunter will be born; and if it is with Ares in Leo, they say that he will be a mighty warrior and a killer.
If Cronus comes into conjunction in Scorpio, someone bitter and ruthless will be born at that hour. From Hermes they seek eloquence,
and from Aphrodite beauty, licentiousness, and good fortune. In this way they bind these things to the revolutions of the wandering and the fixed stars,
and entrust to them the governance of this whole universe. This, then, is the first definition of fate. From this stench,
which these latter-day sons of the pagans inhaled, they declared that fate exists. They agreed in everything with the ancient pagans and denied deeds arising from free will.
They alleged that ruin and restoration, honors and punishments, come about by necessity.

They differed, however, in this: they professed that these things are decreed and predestined by God. They say that everyone is born with it on his head: for each person, they say, it is written from the outset what kind of person
he is to be and how he is to live—whether an unbeliever or a wrongdoer, whether faithful or helpful, whether shameless or full of modesty.
Whether a slave or a worker, whether freeborn or chaste—in short, whether wretched or blessed.
And this comes from necessity. Chance, however, branches out into many different notions and is opposed to fate in every respect.
For they said that it comes either from luck, from an encounter, from coincidence, or from an accident.
Luck is, for example, when someone stumbles and falls in the countryside, or finds treasure, or becomes blind.
They judge such a reversal to lie outside reason and providence, and assign it to good or bad luck. Again, they say:
“So-and-so married a beautiful woman, who rivals the sun and moon in beauty and is full of cleverness and great understanding.”
They call this man fortunate. Another man, while traveling along the road, was robbed of everything he had by a band of robbers,
and they left him naked. They mention him with sighs and say, “Alas, so-and-so is unlucky!”
“Accident” refers to a fall from a roof, an injury, or other wounds that afflict the body.
An “encounter” is, for example, when someone passing through the marketplace is struck with a sword or a staff by a drunkard or a madman and is laid low.
They call such a thing an “accursed encounter” and an “evil meeting.” Coincidence, too, turns out to be similar in kind to these things that have been mentioned.
Chance takes its name figuratively from something like a river in flood, which sweeps away and drags along thick logs and cattle,

and everything it encounters. For example, they say that a certain governor became angry and, while taking vengeance and exacting retribution from those who had offended him, gave orders and roused his troops,
and commanded, “Show no mercy.” When they began exacting retribution, those who had not transgressed became victims of the sword along with the offenders.
They slaughtered the good and the bad indiscriminately, butchered the meek and the savage, and killed friends and enemies alike.
“So-and-so also perished in that same calamity.” The originator of this opinion was the foolish philosopher Epicurus.
For he declared that the world has no maker, that it is eternal and imperishable, enduring and never growing old.

At the same time, he declared that it has no one to care for it or watch over it, but that it came into being by itself, travels without a pilot, and undergoes correction, like a snake that rejuvenates itself
and casts off its old covering through prolonged fasting and through constricting [?]; and like a flying eagle,
which, through the scorching heat of the sun’s rays and through a spring of running water, renews its feathers and rejuvenates its life.
In this way, he said, the world is purified and renewed through floods, fires, and deadly vapors.
Likewise, he said concerning human nature that people have come into being and continue to come into being, and do not come to an end, because they are renewed
through replacement by birth, and that when someone [?], nature brings forth another in his place.
He likewise boldly ventured to speak about the species of animals, the shoots of plants, and the elements’ circulation into one another.
Many, then, inherited this disease—especially the whole brutish herd.
And especially when they fear being caught up in the contemptible doctrine of fate, they have not distinguished which is the royal road and path.
For as we steer our minds through these dangerous pitfalls, we ought not to let the ship of our thought be damaged either by Charybdis or by Scylla.
For this too counsels us in our struggles—namely, shrewd and experienced thinking—to keep far away from both fate and chance.
And we should not, out of fear of fate, say that things happen by chance: when two people are poisoned and have drunk a snake’s gall,
one vomits and escapes, while the other suffers convulsions and his many intestines are torn apart within his belly.
Nor should we adopt that other claim: “It was fated and determined that the man who committed adultery and murder could not have been chaste and peaceable.
It was sealed and decreed.” For both these ways of thinking are unreasonable:
the one which declares that everything happens without reason, and the other which says that everything alike happens through reason and providential care, yet deprives us of the roots of freedom.
Rather, we must assign the workings of providence to the one who stands as overseer of the world, and believe that he gives life and heals.
He grants one person help by taking him out of life, but extends his help to another differently, judging that it is more beneficial for him to remain alive.
But we should leave the things belonging to freedom for freedom itself to perform. It is not, that is,
that they are allotted to it by God and that there is no way for it to undergo them. For if we attribute the actions of freedom to God, and we become like an instrument of his will,
so that we accomplish either evil or good [?], then, first of all, we are led to become like an irrational animal, unrestrained and [?] in our conduct.
And whatever impulse of the desires within us springs up, we cannot refrain from carrying it out.
Next, we are led to despise and disregard the laws. For why should laws be brought to people to whom necessity is yoked,
when it does not allow them to live according to the laws, because their nature runs counter to the excellence of the laws?
Third, they would abandon all education and experience lasting indifference toward every craft or field of knowledge.
The scholar and the elder would not subject the ignorant person and the child to instruction. The smith and the carpenter would not make the nail and the [?], the door and the throne.
For what use are exertion and instruction to someone who, whether he is instructed or not, must inevitably become learned and skilled?
Or why should a carpenter or smith toil and wear himself out, when the implements must come into being in any case, whether he labors or remains idle?
And when lawmaking, education, and craftsmanship are rejected, the administration of justice will also cease. Good men will not be crowned, nor will punishment be imposed on transgressors.
And just as a snake is not [?] when it fasts a great deal, nor an eagle when it spreads its wings wide,
nor are winged creatures praised for lifting their feathers, nor a peacock for its beauty, nor a lion for its strength, nor Behemoth for its size—
for each of them received its distinction from nature and did not choose to be what it is, since it did not exist before it could choose—
so too an ascetic should not be praised and crowned for his fasting and diligence, or for the beauty of his soul and his spiritual struggle. Thus, then.
And let the dissolute person not be blamed, nor the debauched person reproached, just as we do not disparage or reproach the [?] and the fish for their greed and sexual intercourse.
Along with these things, however, they also, for their part, reject thought and deliberation,
and despise them. Still more do those who regard the governance of the great world and human actions as matters of chance. For if,
like a horse deprived of bit and bridle, a person rushes irrationally along with an impulse, galloping here and there and moving swiftly,
and goes wherever the impulse of a nature that loves distraction and amusement leads; and like a ship well equipped upon the flowing water, driven by a wind coming from behind it,
and swept helplessly toward rocks and whirlpools, he is likewise held by some fate that mercilessly diverts the course of our life wherever it wishes—what would happen
if we abandoned the rudder of thought, ceased our efforts, and were stripped of its fruits? Let us not consider marrying, or sowing, or plowing.
Rather, let us mate in our sleep, without knowing it, and like cattle and wild asses let us draw our nourishment from the earth with sharp teeth.
In short, let all our actions be performed by us without knowledge and without understanding. Consequently, let the very activity of contemplation be despised and regarded as futile.
But let these things dwell far from us. For, since we were created capable of thought, it is utterly foolish for our actions to proceed by chance.
And since we were constituted free, it is also contemptible for us to be subjected to the compulsion of fate.
But those who act as advocates for chance and for the course of nature say: “Look, we rejoice that certain causes follow from nature and exceed their limits.
Sometimes they cause a great deal of damage and destruction, while at other times they provide much assistance to crops and plants.
Nature brings one condition or another upon the inhabited world and its inhabitants. For example, those winds that have come to dwell in the depths of the earth,
when they increase and grow strong, cause cities to shake and tremble. As a result, many people are hurled down to Sheol.

But in other places, when they grow strong, they emerge from their underground hollows, and as they emerge they cause springs of water to flow. Along with this account of nature, the air also comes into consideration.
It grows cold and sends many blights. For many days it covers everything with ice and damages the things growing upon the earth.
But in those southern regions [?], fierce heat lays things low, strips the stalks of grain of their produce, and harms the trees, both their blossoms and their fruit.
It causes countless other losses when it becomes intensely heated and boils from the strength of the sun in summer.
Along with these things, the inhabitants of the south are long-lived, while those in the north lead difficult and short lives.
In one climate, they say, beauty reigns, but in another, a repulsive appearance.” These and other similar things are said
by those who act as advocates for chance and have every argument ready on behalf of nature. But what do we answer them? Surely this:
From him who fills the world, our entire nature comes and is governed, both in these customary conditions and in departures from these customary conditions.
He fittingly produces constancy and stability in the elements, in animals, and in every kind of plant, looking toward the immediate benefit that abundance provides for human beings.
He also produces many changes and variations, both in the elements and in these other things, looking toward what is more beneficial.
For this reason he joined certain causes to nature, so that, when we become entangled in the snares of sin, we may be harmed by them.
But when we conduct ourselves properly, not only will we suffer no harm from them, but we will also receive great help.
For this reason he allows the region beneath Olympus to be shaken by winds.
He lets the winds of the air loose, allowing them to damage [?] the sprouting crops through blights and frosts; and he does not restrain the brilliance of the sun’s rays,
when they grow hot and blazing and bring about great dangers. He loosens the sea’s boundary, and it sweeps away the inhabitants of the land. These things he does—

he who commands the sun and it does not rise, who brings winds out of his storehouses, who in the beginning set sand as a boundary for the sea, who suspended the earth upon nothing, and who can accomplish everything by a mere gesture of his will.
For when our mind lapses into the disorder of sin, he lets the world’s restraints go, and it too passes into destruction and disorder.
And furthermore, through the very things for which we gave no thanks when we were honored, and through which we did not advance toward virtue, we are also to be disciplined,
and learn his power from what we suffer, since we did not recognize it from the good things that happened to us, as the Theologian says.
For this reason he allows the winds that dwell in the recesses of the earth to shake the inhabited world, overturn cities, and destroy their inhabitants. As the blessed Ephrem said, the earth became
higher than the evildoer, he says, because it could not bear to remain beneath him. And the great David says: “He looks at the earth and it trembles; he rebukes the mountains and they smoke.”
The following will show that nature, even when it is left loose and released from the restraints of providence, is kept from some lapse into disorder. For there is a certain great mountain.
Trembling and shaking occur in it continually, yet we know that it never harms its inhabitants—perhaps because they do not deserve destruction.
Indeed, if the movement and force of the wind were not restrained by the one who watches over the world, the wind’s violence would never allow its inhabitants to live there.
But another place, where no wind had accumulated at all, was unexpectedly shaken by the wind’s violence, and many people perished there.
A few people, however, unexpectedly found deliverance. In this place, through the watchful care of grace, one man who had been buried beneath the rubble for eleven days
was brought out by men who buried the dead, as though from the [?] of Sheol, after his groaning showed them where he lay. Likewise, we have also heard concerning the sea
that, although it surges mightily, rolls in waves year after year, and gathers tremendous force, it has not swept away or harmed the neighboring land,
because the law of life restrains and checks it. But in a place where, at a gesture, it found its restraint loosened, it prepared great destruction for cities and the islands within it.
And when the sun grew scorching hot, it stupefied many creatures and damaged the fruit-bearing power of plants.

These causes, and others like them, the one who brings everything into being has bound together with the whole of nature, so that through these same experiences people may enjoy well-being when they act rightly, but be handed over to suffering when they turn aside and sin.
Everywhere and in every place, whatever has been set apart and given by God for help and enjoyment, he turns into distress when sin reigns.
And just as he provides beneficial composition and growth through nourishment for all bodies, to which, after the four [?], he gave their beginning from the four,
so too he either permits, allows, or brings about their breaking apart, dispersal, arrest [?], and deprivation through those very same things. Thus a tract of cultivated land,
in which stalks of grain grow thickly, he makes barren through scorching heat and drought; and through famine he judges and chastises its inhabitants. And again, where there is pasture
[?] it is; and, though rich and luxuriant in gardens and forests, he strikes down and lays low its inhabitants through deadly vapors.

From the air above them he brings about the destruction of many of them. In some places he does so through swarms of creeping creatures and locusts, which the earth spews out and the air carries without warning or expectation.
He cuts off their prosperity along with their lives. In short, everywhere and in every place, whatever is set apart for pleasure is dispatched for torment.
But perhaps someone will say, “We see that in a certain place [?] many people died when the annual epidemic engulfed its inhabitants.
Yet some of them were saved by going away to the mountain.” It seems to me that whoever says this knows nothing at all about the power of God.
For the great David, praising him, said concerning this: “If I ascend to heaven, you are there; and if I descend to Sheol, you are there too.
If I raise my wings like an eagle and settle at the farthest end of the sea, even there your hand will hold me, and your right hand will guide me.”
Another prophet, speaking about the Israelites who wanted to distance themselves from God's yoke and were harnessing themselves beneath the burden of the Assyrians and Egyptians,
said as though speaking in the Lord's own person: “He came to Egypt and went to Assyria. Wherever they go, I will spread my net over them.”
Yet another said: “Just as someone might go out into the countryside and encounter a bear, then enter the house, rest his hand against the wall, and be bitten by a snake, so is the day of the Lord:
dark and not light.” For such is the power of the Lord when it rises against the wicked.
For when a town or city receives correction as punishment, I pity the person who wants to escape and be saved.
“For the earth and everything that fills it belong to the Lord,” says the singer of sacred songs. If not in this place, he catches him in another, and he no longer escapes the net of destruction,
unless, perhaps, he clings to the law of righteousness and takes refuge in the covenants of holiness, as also happened in the case of priestly Jerusalem.
For when they defiled their way of life and provoked the Holy One of Israel to anger in their sanctuary and their priesthood [?], through mighty angels
their end came upon them. Only those escaped judgment who, through the care of the one clothed in linen, received a mark between their eyes,
which indicated their obedience to the law and their purity. But if someone found deliverance from a place being devastated by moving away from that place,
as did those who escaped the epidemic by going up to the mountain, we say that a remnant of virtue and a leaven of repentance were found in that person.
He escaped both the place and the judgment when God stirred him, or a holy angel led him, or his conscience moved him. He changed his location and found life.
He was not cut down by the sickle swung against the wicked. For the sharpened sword and the drunken blade
drain away the blood of the righteous together with that of the wicked, teaching us not to love living among evil people, which infects the conduct of many.
For this reason, through the mission of angels, he removed righteous Lot and brought him out of the unclean place.
He also calls his people and draws them away from the wicked Babylonians, saying through the prophet: “Flee, flee from Babylon!
Do not come near it. Everyone found in it will be pierced by the sword, because the Lord desires that his will be done in Babylon and in the land of the Chaldeans.”
The Lord does this out of grace and compassion for the righteous: he removes them and brings them out of the place being ravaged by destruction, and away from the angel of death.
He shields him and shelters him. Either through a holy vision, through a guardian angel, or through a prophet and seer, he moves him away from there,
as we have said. But if he flees from a place under wrath and judgment by the freedom of his own will, either he finds no escape at all,

if he does not desist from his wickedness, or, if he does find escape, there was a good thought in his heart, on account of which he shook and jolted even the place. I mean that he should persevere in goodness
and produce the fruits of repentance. That some people escape death does not happen randomly or by chance. Otherwise, establish this:
some individuals escape death and destruction from pestilence even while they dwell in that very place,
whereas others perish and die even after moving away, either from that same disease or in some other way.
We also observe something similar concerning other chastisements, such as locusts or hail.
For when the good angels, who are appointed to guard us, benefit us, or turn us back, are sent to pronounce some judgment against us,
so that they may turn us back from the error of wickedness, they providentially bring hail or locusts upon the produce of their fields. We see this happening:

a cloud bearing hailstones, while speeding through one place, does no harm at all. Yet within a single district, in one field—the wicked man's field—it pours down, and the field is immediately battered by hail.
But the righteous man's field escapes. We have also heard of two villages situated beside one another in the same locality and district:
the produce of one suffered complete destruction from hail all at once, while the other was not harmed in any way.
What is remarkable is that the cloud is guided by an angel like a twisting serpent. He sets it moving from the west, and after it has struck one village, it passes by another.
It rises toward the north, and after destroying other villages there, it lashes others toward the east or the south.
It leaves many in between without loss or injury. Here one can marvel and see the working of nature,
how it ceases and stands still because of providential governance. For most clouds, whenever winds draw them from the west or the east,
are guided along a straight path. They pour down their droplets and water the earth. We have heard the same concerning locusts.
For when the guardian angel set the swarm in motion and devastated many districts with it, he handed it over to destruction at the boundary of another region.
The scourge that had crushed many he crushed and cast down with another stronger than itself. For he unleashed a mighty wind against it and first crippled it so that it could not enter the region.
Then, through a cloud bearing hailstones, he struck it down and wiped it out, leaving it like heaps of those killed by the sword.
The guardian angel saved the region and all its inhabitants. “Let these things,” he says, “be as you have said.
But what answer will you give to that other point concerning those whom, because of the favorable conditions or bad climate of their locations, nature has made long-lived
and ugly in appearance, while it has assigned others a precarious life and little strength? Likewise, other regions rear people who are quick and vigorous because of their favorable conditions.
And so that our discussion does not become drawn out as these things are recalled one by one: concerning all those who live in some part of this whole world,
whose lives are either shortened or prolonged, who are beautiful or ugly, licentious or chaste, or concerning the way of life in each region or the customs of peoples—what, then?”
The law of providence has vanished for it, and nature itself brings things about or is brought along [?]—no longer! Rather, nature itself runs according to the command of its Creator.
As for human beings, their lives are measured out for them according to what is beneficial, by God. But they determine their dwelling according to their own judgment and wherever they wish.
That it is not the sun that measures out the Ethiopians’ lives is shown by this: among them too, young men pass into Sheol, and infants are snatched away from life.
And sometimes, through a great plague, many cities and many people pass away.
Or are there really places among them where no young man has passed into Sheol, and no fetus or infant has died before its time?
I think this is altogether false. For, as far as everyone is concerned, the bonds by which the world is held are tightened around them in the same way.
In the north too, the lives of its inhabitants are measured out according to what is beneficial. Among them, old people too are found [?] through the hand of providence.
As for beauty and understanding, together with keenness and strength, which are found in different places, we attribute them to favorable conditions.
For free will, if it chooses to bring a person into those regions where the sun’s heat is intense, is not prevented.
When it settles him there, it makes his complexion [?] and ugly, his body thin and parched; and from this he becomes [?].
Free will has guided another person and allotted him a dwelling in temperate regions. Brought up in shade and coolness, he has turned out handsome and beautiful in complexion.
Yet even when free will acts in this way, unless help comes from providence on high, beauty turns to ugliness, whether through illness or through
some other cause. Strength grows weak, and the mind becomes bewildered and foolish. It constrains the favorable conditions of places and dwellings,
and casts them into trials and adversities, driving them away from the advantages proper to them. That great King delights in these things,
as he governs the world wherever he wishes and leads it this way and that according to what is beneficial, in everything working for the benefit of our lives.

He placed certain causes within nature, which gives birth to everything, so that with them and through them the lives of earthly creatures might proceed. He appointed the sun as the chief source of light.
He bound the soul to blood and marrow. Yet because a change in these things brings about a change in the soul, we are not led to say that they are the soul’s creators.
Likewise, even if nature has been allotted a certain capacity to bring one thing about in one way and another in another way, we do not deprive the Maker of the world of the reins of government.
Rather, as we ought to acknowledge, we are obliged to bind nature itself, together with its operations, to the hand of its Maker. So much for these matters.
This is the explanation. If it is sufficient, thanks be to the one who granted it. If not, let someone else who loves hard work enter into other arguments and help our discussion.
For our part, let us now turn to other questions and examine them according to our ability.
It is clear that, while we were dealing with simple matters, something fell short of our undertaking. Antony said:
“Tell me, you Spirit who dwell in the high heavens, who hold the limits of the great world, who rest upon the holy ones and grant them eyes that can see:
“What explains this: when two men were traveling on foot along the road [?], and a great calamity came upon them, with sulfurous lightning bolts bursting forth,
“one of them perished, while the other found a final escape? Spirit, through the mouth of a holy man, [?] this to me.”
For the Lord knew beforehand and in advance that the man who perished would never repent and would gain nothing from his companion’s punishment, so he put him to death.
But he knew that fear would terrify the man who remained, restrain him from wickedness, bring him toward repentance, and show him the fruits of repentance.
Again Antony wondered whether the man struck by lightning received any benefit from the repentance and virtue of the man

who remained. Again the Spirit, who brings mysteries, enlightened him through another person: “If, of two sinners, one is struck so that the other may recoil in fear, it is just for God to make their benefit common to both,
so that the punishment of the one who was struck and the repentance of the one who was afraid are brought together, placed in their common midst, and divided into shares.” Again he investigated this:
why one man, though struck and subjected to countless swords and lashes, escaped ravenous death, while another who saw battle went down to Sheol from fear.
And concerning this, from a mind that considered what was just [?], he spoke and established it as something beneficial and helpful. For the Father appointed swords and lashes as a help for that man.
Or have you not seen [?] many who reached the harbors of holiness because of the sufferings that came through discipline? But he helped this man through the manner of his departure.
For he knew that his life would produce loss and harm if he continued living in this passing world. Hence, one man, though severely afflicted by pain
and calling Sheol his mother, he did not take out of life. But another he took and removed while life was still pleasant to him and he had abundant provisions for his journey.
Again it was asked why he allows the oppressive and unjust person a long life and permits him to live a sinful life. To this he replied:
“So that, as with a bitter rod, he may cleanse many from wickedness through their hands.” Thus we sometimes see among human lawyers
that, after they had devoured people who lacked strength and deprived the wretched and orphans of houses and fields, another unjust man came upon them,
pressed them with great plunder, and reduced them to [?]. Again I saw something else, and I recount it for the benefit of many:
the Word, full of justice, allowed and permitted an entire regiment, although heavily armed, to fall into the hands of weak men, who brought about their destruction and annihilation.
That regiment was entirely wicked. For when, from the land of the Assyrians,
some men, contemptible in their trades and petty in their deeds, armed themselves against the barbarians, they recklessly undertook to violate their women like mares
and to have no pity on them or on the children of their wombs. But the Lord strengthened those unsociable men who loved devastation, and they brought about the regiment’s destruction.
