For their long-standing wickedness they received a single repayment: slaughter at barbarian hands. Again, concerning infants who die before their time, as we express it,
Antony sought an explanation. For this he found five reasons in brief, according to the teaching of the fathers. The first: when he rebukes an unrighteous conception.
For, they say, he judged David and killed his son as a child of adultery, so that this fruit would not become a destructive example to many.
The second: if he sees crafty love of money flourishing and increasing among parents because of the children born to them.
For we also see many who perish through worry and concern about money and make their children the excuse. Others, however, acquire possessions even though they have no children.
The former are reproved by the latter, and the latter by the former, showing that children are not the cause of this passion.
The third: when he sees their wickedness and honors a righteous father, so that the fruit of sin may not flourish.
Fourth: if they are destined to become more unjust than anyone else, and thoroughly accomplished in wickedness.
Fifth: how, for that heavenly assembly, [?] through [?]; and for this reason he takes them as sinless and worthy of that wedding feast, so that he may not lack them,
and so that none may be missing from the complete number of the hundred sheep. The saints stated these reasons. Either for that reason, or for this one, or perhaps for another,
or possibly for this reason or that, God removes the infant from the course of life here.

But if someone hesitates over these words as though they were insufficient, let him lower the line of his thought into the unsearchable judgments, and let him too hear what was said to Antony the Great.
For when he earnestly pleaded that the Lord would show him why this departure from life sometimes happens to infants, this answer was given to him:
“Antony, know yourself, but do not investigate my judgments.” Hence we too qualify the reason for our explanation with “perhaps,” “possibly,” or “[?].”
And thus we have not put forward the explanation on our own authority. Antony says: “I decided, as a particular help for myself, to take up wealth and poverty as well,
and to say, according to my limited ability, whether all wealth comes from God. For I have heard many people ask this, and this very question is asked of me and of others.
Some wealth is provided through providence and help from above, from God; other wealth comes through his allowing things to happen and through free will. As for what comes through free will,
some comes through care and effort, whether in commerce or in crafts, while some comes through acts of oppression.
Other wealth comes from the devil; other wealth comes from coincidence and chance, with God allowing it.
He allows and permits it if it does not harm its possessor. But if it does harm him, it is so that free will may be put under pressure and tested.
For many people, when they are worn down by the bitterness and hardships of poverty and look at the rich with a bitter eye full of envy, say,
“If God had given me wealth, I would have managed it in a wonderfully beneficial way.” Consequently, God allows this to happen to them,
judging their free will and its words, since it does not, in fact, turn away from its wickedness. But so that my discussion may not wander from its purpose,
I will return and distinguish, by examples, the main categories of the division already mentioned. Some wealth is given by God, like that of the righteous.

Thus the great man of the Hebrews said about Isaac: “He sowed in that [?] and brought in a hundredfold yield of barley; and the Lord blessed him, and the man became great”—the great man of the Hebrews.
And again, concerning Job: “The Lord doubled everything he had,” and there are others like these.
Wealth from a craft and manual work is like that of people who cast statues or skillfully make things for kings,
for which large payments are weighed out. Farmers, builders, carpenters, arrow sharpeners, sword polishers, and weavers acquire wealth in this way,
and, in short, every craft and trade through which its practitioners become useful, double their profits, and increase their possessions.
Such people include [?], that is, money changers, and those who travel from place to place for business abroad, whether by ships or by caravans, and others like them.
Wealth from commerce is accompanied by diligence, concern, and a measure of toil, though not in the same way as for craftsmen.

Rather, shrewdness, astuteness, considerable ingenuity, and adaptability benefit it more than anything else. And when free will itself takes care and acts resourcefully, it is never restrained by God.
Even though sometimes, and for some people, it is as a certain philosopher said: “There is someone who tires himself out, runs, and toils, yet in all these things he falls behind,” and so on.
Sin also accompanies commerce, as someone else said: “Sins press in between buying and selling, just as a peg goes in between one stone and another.”
And a shopkeeper is not free from sins: he constantly engages in oaths and falsehood and continually practices hidden, unseen acts of fraud.
The fourth kind of wealth is that gathered through oppression and robbery, such as the wealth of governors and their legal officials, and that of robbers and brigands.
This wealth does not usually last, because it is mixed with other people’s tears, and sometimes even with the blood of their relatives.
As the wise man also said: “Possessions gained through injustice will diminish, but what is gathered through righteousness will increase.” And as the victorious Job said:
“I have seen a wicked man prospering, but suddenly his dwelling perished. His children will be far from the commandments,” and similar things.
The fifth kind of wealth is that gathered through demons, such as the wealth of sorcerers and Chaldeans,
necromancers, men who practice divination, foretellers of the future, enchanters, astrologers, and stargazers.
For their wealth is gathered from the wages of sin and from the demon who reveals the riches of many people. How, for example?
Someone was traveling, and his cargo was taken away by brigands. He came to a sorcerer and promised him a thousand pieces of silver, or half his cargo.
Now Satan, the father of sin, who stirred up the robber to take courage at the crossing and rob him, knows who robbed the merchant, whether in a house or on the road.
He therefore reveals it to the Chaldean. And when the deed wins praise, the man is given what he requested.
In the same way, demons also show their fully trained disciples treasures buried in the earth.
And if, after receiving these things, they later wish to turn toward the Lord and remove their former slavery from their necks,
he takes the treasures away and retrieves them through plunder, whether by brigands, rulers, or some other means.
For this reason he does not give or entrust to many sorcerers the hidden treasures stored in the chambers of the earth, lest they be freed from need
and escape his unjust yoke. Instead, he continually afflicts them with anxiety and want, so that they will remain enslaved to him and labor in his service. Hence there are also
Chaldeans who are needy. But why, when my intention is to explain the causes of wealth, toward poverty and want
have I been carried away and descended? The sixth kind of wealth is what people say comes about through chance and good fortune,
when permission is given by the one who holds dominion, as a test of free will. For example, someone digging a deep channel
or excavating a well might find a treasure of gold or silver; or someone might be tending donkeys or cattle in deserted places.
And as they say about the fisherman who, after selling fish to some young men, drew up and hauled in with his net a golden [?] with three legs.
And as they say about the king of the Samians, whose ancestral ring fell into the [?] waters and the deep recesses of the sea:
soon afterward, a fisherman unknowingly sold it to the royal household inside a fish. Such finds, and others like them.
They give wealth and happiness to many. And all things are acquired either through the hand of abandonment or through the hand that cares for everything.
These are the general kinds and principal categories through which material wealth is amassed for the inhabitants of the earth and, for the most part, accumulated.
For individuals, however, we find that wealth can be acquired apart from these kinds already mentioned, as in the case of a tutor or a priest,
or a lyre singer, or a son of Tubal-Cain, or a woman practicing the trade of Aphrodite, or a powerful counselor, or a [?] who, in the guise of a champion,
takes bribes from the powerful. Sometimes, however, people offer many tokens of affection to someone who is good at his craft and priestly in his conduct.
From this, great wealth comes into his hands. We have seen a wealthy wearer of the monastic habit, just as we have also observed a greedy leader.
For me, however, every kind of wealth is bound in the chain of greed, apart from the initial impulse, whereby it is either given by God or acquired through toil.
The rest, in my judgment, are bonds of injustice, deserving the fire of the people of Sodom. And do not tell me that so-and-so is a chief priest, or that so-and-so is a scholar.
For if his heart and his hand are stained by silver or by the moneybag, he is, in my judgment, a wretched man and a son of the left.
These, then, are the kinds of wealth. Poverty, however, has three divisions. The first is the furnace of testing that God kindles against a person, either
to test him, as with the good, or to discipline his stubbornness, as with the wicked. For money is material for all sorts of base deeds, though not for every one of them.
For this reason, the Lord himself either prevents a person from acquiring it or subsequently strips it away from us.
The second kind is what comes upon a poor person through slackness of hand and laziness. The third comes from free choice.
This last kind extends into many areas. The first and good form among them is that in which, for the glory of heavenly wealth
and the hope of rewards in the world beyond, a person resolves to become poor, as with Elijah’s need and the poverty of the apostles.
The second and evil form is that which a person’s shameful desires bring upon him, as with bands of drunkards and companies of lovers of [?],
who have squandered inherited possessions and the treasures of industrious people to fill the belly’s gluttonous abyss with wine and exhaust their resources on the cavern of desire for Eve.

They are left without what they had accumulated, yet have not attained what they desired and loved. For drinking wine increases drunkenness, and the flame of desire burns all the more when it is satisfied.
The third kind of need, which is something intermediate, neither evil nor good, concerns those who, for the vain praise of the world [?],
become generous beyond measure and spend everything they have before people’s eyes, so that they may win praise from everyone.
Since this kind does not arise for the sake of goodness itself, it is not classified as good. Yet because it brings benefit and fruit to many, it is not called evil either.
Nevertheless, we and all those in the church call this kind evil. These are the kinds of poverty.
But if there is some other circumstance through which that wretched poor person experiences the misery of want—whether the harshness of a tax collector,
or a disastrous year that deprives the fields of their produce, or an illness affecting an individual who practiced a trade and was impoverished because of it,
or an attack someone suffers through the wickedness of thieves or robbers—all these and similar cases are to be placed in those first two categories of need.
I mean, either to examine or to acquire. We have therefore distinguished and explained these kinds,
so that, when the mind receives them, it will not say that all wealth comes from God and make God an accomplice of robbers, Chaldeans, and oppressive men.
For he gave us freedom of will and established power within it. He leaves it free until he judges it, so that whenever it wishes it may [?], and may say and do whatever it wishes.
He does not restrain the robber when his unjust hand is raised against another person's wealth, knowing that he is estranged more by wealth than by need and misery.
If someone makes poverty material for blasphemy, he takes it away and gives him abundance instead. But if someone is a grumbler, and he knows that, when he becomes rich,
he will kill, commit adultery, and perpetrate other outrages, he leaves him bound in that very chain of poverty. Another person, for whom wealth is suitable,
and who becomes an honest steward of money, compassionate and merciful in his intentions and in his actions—he increases and blesses everything that person possesses.
He extends his abundance through the succession of generation after generation. But when, after his death, his children act foolishly and take the money inherited from their righteous father
and make it material for their sin, he takes it away. He bends and bows them beneath the hard-to-bear yoke of poverty,
which is hateful and repulsive to everyone alike: frightening before they experience it, something to flee after they experience it, and painful to remember when we have escaped it.
But there are many who, when they are crushed beneath the yoke of need and experience its bitter sufferings,
and how hard it is to be humbled before many people, remember that experience when they become prosperous. To these the Lord gives wealth,
because, as the one who knows everything, he knows that the memory of misery will draw them toward compassion for their fellow human beings.
But he knows other poor people whom the memory of poverty causes to keep a clenched and unyielding hand upon their purse,
and in whom the memory of the sufferings of need stirs up an aversion to mercy. For this reason, he does not undertake to lift that yoke from them.
Through these opposites, and through others like them—I mean sickness and health,
weakness and strength, sharpness of the senses and impairment, shrewdness and simplicity, beauty and neediness, authority and subjection, or mastery and slavery—
through these and whatever other opposites there are, that all-knowing navigator judges, guiding and directing human nature this way and that, and in every direction,
but always toward what brings salvation and is greatly beneficial. Rather, then, let us give thanks, and at every turn offer a tribute of thanksgiving and a pure sacrifice of praise,
magnifying him in astonishment and wonder, and saying these things with amazement:
O sower and founder of the world! O holder of the rudders and navigator of this whole universe! O guide and director of the human mind and understanding,
and maker of thoughts! O Mind utterly beyond understanding, Word that eludes words, and Spirit who established the immaterial spirits!
O God of human beings, who belong to you, their Lord and merciful Father! O blessed one beyond measure, and fountain of all compassion!
You who watch over our affairs with justice and grace, yet give grace the upper hand,
and guide freedom along the path of providence, and, treating it as your own image, free it from the anxieties of oppression!
And you alone, like a good physician of evils, cleanse it from the defilement of shameful deeds; and like a contemplator and examiner of contemplation, you correct its errors in contemplation.
O founder of the great city, Father and Maker of the worlds to come, who gives wisdom and illumination to all beings,
who, having been brought into existence in you, also continue to exist in you at every moment, and to whom abundant nourishment is extended from you and through your hands.
O Radiance equal to your begetter, in whom the good powers are illuminated and rejoice, drawing knowledge from the fountain of rays,
they also grant that we may be illuminated and shine, pour forth some of the light of knowledge, and pass it on to another, O Threefold and Only One,
you who, in your entirety, together with everything that comes from you, remain beyond our lowliness, while we receive from you only as much of your dealings with us as we can bear.

At times, however, we are also deemed worthy to comprehend what wonders, and of what kind, you have done and are doing in us and for us, provided that we too show ourselves worthy of this here, and through love of toil
